**Who can grant**: Cloud Application Administrator and Application Administrator can grant most consent. Granting **Microsoft Graph application permissions** needs Privileged Role Administrator or Global Administrator.
**Admin consent workflow** (Consent and permissions > **Admin consent settings**):
- **Users can request admin consent to apps they are unable to consent to** = Yes
- **Who can review admin consent requests**: users, groups or roles
- Email notifications and expiry reminders
- **Consent request expires after (days)**.
The user submits a justification from the consent prompt. Reviewers see it under **Admin consent requests** and can approve, deny or block it. Being a reviewer **doesn't grant** consent rights. Reviewers still need a role that can grant the requested permissions. Configuring the workflow requires Global Administrator.

terms.d: Tenant-wide approval of an app's permissions on behalf of all users.
Lets an app act as itself with no signed-in user; always requires admin consent.
Lets users request admin consent and routes the request to designated reviewers.

lessons.trap: Designating someone as a reviewer doesn't let them approve everything. They still need a role that can grant the requested permissions.
lessons.example: A marketer requests consent for a survey app that needs Mail.Send. A Cloud Application Administrator reviewer checks the publisher and approves it.

lessons.title: Application collections in My Apps
lessons.short: Collections group apps into named tabs in the My Apps portal, such as 'HR tools' or 'Sales'. Admins create them in Enterprise apps > App launchers, add apps, set owners, and assign the collection to users or groups. Users see only the apps in a collection that they already have access to.
lessons.deep:
The **My Apps** portal (`myapps.microsoft.com`) shows every app a user is assigned. In large tenants that becomes cluttered. **Collections** organize it.
**Create a collection**: Microsoft Entra admin center > **Enterprise apps** > **App launchers** > **New collection**:
1. Enter a name (for example 'Finance'), and a description.
2. **Applications** tab: add apps and set their order.
3. **Owners** tab: add users who can manage the collection.
4. **Users and groups** tab: assign the collection to the users or groups who should see the tab.
5. **Review + Create**.
**Key facts**
- Requires **Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2**.
- Roles: **Cloud Application Administrator** or **Application Administrator** (or an owner).
- A collection is a **filter, not an assignment**. It never grants access to an app. Users see only the collection's apps that they're already assigned. If an app is missing, assign the user to the app itself.
- Admin collections are managed in the admin center, not in My Apps. Users can also organize their own view in My Apps.
- Create, edit and delete events appear in the Enterprise apps **audit logs** under the My Apps service.

terms.d: The end-user portal listing apps a user can launch, at myapps.microsoft.com.
An admin-defined tab in My Apps that groups related applications.
The Enterprise apps blade where collections are created and managed.

lessons.trap: Adding an app to a collection doesn't give users access. They must also be assigned to the app.
lessons.example: The Sales collection holds the CRM, quoting and e-signature apps and is assigned to the Sales group, so sellers see one focused tab.

lessons.title: Planning app registrations
lessons.short: An app registration creates an application object, the global definition of an app in its home tenant. Each tenant that uses the app gets a service principal, its local instance. When you plan, pick the supported account types (single tenant or multitenant), who may register apps, which credential type to use, and the permission model.
lessons.deep:
**Application object vs service principal**
- The **application object** (App registrations blade) exists only in the **home tenant**. It works like a template: name, redirect URIs, credentials, the APIs it exposes, app roles and requested permissions.
- A **service principal** (Enterprise apps blade) is created in **every tenant** that uses the app, at registration in the home tenant or at consent in other tenants. Assignments, consent grants and Conditional Access apply to it.
- The relationship is one-to-many: one application object and many service principals. Managed identity service principals have no application object.
**Supported account types** (`signInAudience`):
- **Single tenant** (AzureADMyOrg): recommended for most line-of-business apps.
- **Multitenant** (AzureADMultipleOrgs): SaaS for any Entra tenant.
- **Multitenant + personal Microsoft accounts** (AzureADandPersonalMicrosoftAccount).
- **Personal accounts only** (PersonalMicrosoftAccount).
**Planning decisions**: who can register (the tenant setting plus the Application Developer role), naming and ownership standards (at least two owners), **credential type** (federated credential > certificate > secret), **delegated vs application** permissions, whether to define **app roles**, and whether to require assignment. Also plan **publisher verification** for multitenant apps so users can consent under verified-publisher policies.

terms.d: The global definition of an app, stored only in its home tenant (App registrations).
The manifest property for supported account types, such as AzureADMyOrg or AzureADMultipleOrgs.
The tenant where the app was registered and where its application object lives.

lessons.trap: Candidates think a multitenant app copies its application object into each customer tenant. Only a service principal is created there.
lessons.example: Adatum registers a multitenant HR app in its own tenant. When Contoso's admin consents, a service principal for the app appears in Contoso's Enterprise apps.

lessons.title: Creating app registrations
lessons.short: Create a registration in Entra ID > App registrations > New registration. Enter a name, choose the supported account types and optionally a redirect URI. Record the Application (client) ID and the Directory (tenant) ID. You can automate the same thing with New-MgApplication, az ad app create, or Graph POST /applications.
lessons.deep:
**Portal**: Microsoft Entra admin center > **Entra ID** > **App registrations** > **New registration**.
1. **Name**: the display name users see on consent prompts.
2. **Supported account types**.
3. **Redirect URI** (optional now): choose a platform and URI.
4. **Register**.
The **Overview** page shows:
- **Application (client) ID** (`appId`): identifies the app in code and token requests.
- **Object ID**: the ID of the application object itself. It's different from the service principal's object ID.
- **Directory (tenant) ID**.
**Automation**
- Microsoft Graph PowerShell: `New-MgApplication -DisplayName 'Orders API' -SignInAudience AzureADMyOrg`, then `New-MgServicePrincipal -AppId <appId>` if needed.
- Azure CLI: `az ad app create --display-name 'Orders API'` and `az ad sp create --id <appId>`.
- Graph API: `POST https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/applications`.
Registering in the portal also creates the home tenant's service principal automatically. **Prerequisite**: the 'Users can register applications' setting must allow it, or you need Application Developer or a higher role. The creator becomes an **owner**. After creation, configure authentication, credentials, API permissions, an exposed API (Application ID URI `api://<client-id>`) and app roles.

terms.d: The appId GUID that identifies an app in token requests; the same in every tenant.
The directory object's own ID; the application object and each service principal have different object IDs.
Microsoft Graph PowerShell cmdlet that creates an application object.

lessons.trap: The application object's Object ID is offered where the client ID is needed, such as in MSAL configuration. Code uses the Application (client) ID.
lessons.example: A DevOps engineer runs New-MgApplication in a pipeline to create 'Orders API' as single tenant, then adds a federated credential for GitHub.

lessons.title: Configuring app authentication: platforms and redirect URIs
lessons.short: On the Authentication blade, add a platform (Web, Single-page application, iOS/macOS, Android, or Mobile and desktop) with its redirect URIs, where Entra ID sends tokens. You can also set a front-channel logout URL. Avoid the implicit grant and use authorization code flow with PKCE. Enable public client flows only when needed.
lessons.deep:
**Redirect URI (reply URL)**: after sign-in, Entra ID sends the authorization code or tokens **only** to a URI registered on the app. This stops tokens being sent to an attacker's site. URIs must use HTTPS, except `http://localhost`.
**Platforms**
- **Web**: server-side apps (ASP.NET, Node) that are confidential clients with a secret or certificate.
- **Single-page application (SPA)**: browser JavaScript apps (React, Angular). Uses **authorization code flow with PKCE**, with no secret.
- **iOS / macOS** and **Android**: the redirect URI is generated from the bundle ID or the package name plus signature hash.
- **Mobile and desktop applications**: native clients, such as `https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/nativeclient`.
**Other settings**
- **Front-channel logout URL**: where Entra ID sends sign-out so the app clears its session.
- **Implicit grant and hybrid flows**: check boxes for **ID tokens** and **Access tokens**. Leave them off for new apps. Implicit flow is no longer recommended because browsers are removing third-party cookies, so use auth code flow.
- **Allow public client flows**: enables device code flow and ROPC (resource owner password credentials) for public clients.
- Supported account types can also be changed here.

terms.d: A registered endpoint where the identity platform sends codes or tokens after authentication.
Proof Key for Code Exchange: protects authorization code flow for public clients like SPAs and mobile apps.
A legacy flow returning tokens directly from /authorize; discouraged in favor of auth code flow.

lessons.trap: For a new SPA, enabling the implicit grant check boxes is offered. The right answer is the SPA platform with authorization code flow and PKCE.
lessons.example: A React app registered under the Single-page application platform with https://app.contoso.com/auth uses MSAL.js and PKCE, with implicit grant left unchecked.

lessons.title: App credentials: certificates, secrets and federated credentials
lessons.short: Confidential apps prove their identity with a credential. Federated credentials (workload identity federation) need no secret at all. Certificates are the recommended stored credential. Client secrets are the weakest and last at most 24 months. Microsoft recommends under 12 months. Manage them under Certificates & secrets.
lessons.deep:
**Certificates & secrets** blade on the app registration:
- **Certificates**: upload the public key (`.cer`, `.pem` or `.crt`). The app signs a client assertion with the private key. Recommended over secrets. In production, use a CA-signed certificate managed in **Azure Key Vault**.
- **Client secrets**: a generated string (an application password). The value is **shown only once**. The maximum lifetime is **24 months**, and Microsoft recommends less than 12 months and not using secrets in production.
- **Federated credentials**: **workload identity federation**. The app (or a **user-assigned managed identity**) trusts tokens from an external OIDC identity provider and swaps them for Entra tokens with no stored secret. Scenarios include **GitHub Actions**, **Kubernetes** service accounts, Google Cloud, AWS and other issuers.
  - The trust matches the external token's **issuer**, **subject** and **audience** (default `api://AzureADTokenExchange`) **exactly and case-sensitively**.
  - Up to **20** federated credentials per app or user-assigned managed identity.
  - Tokens issued by Microsoft Entra ID itself can't be used as the external token.
Governance tips: track expiry with Entra recommendations and workload identity sign-in logs, and use app management policies to restrict secrets or their lifetimes. Workload ID Premium licensing adds Conditional Access and ID Protection for service principals.

terms.d: Trusting an external IdP's tokens so a workload gets Entra tokens without a secret.
The trust object (issuer, subject, audiences) on an app or user-assigned managed identity.
A password-like string for an app; maximum 24 months, shown only once.

lessons.trap: For GitHub Actions deploying to Azure, the 'secure' answer is not a certificate stored in GitHub secrets. It's a federated credential with no stored secret.
lessons.example: A GitHub workflow on the main branch of contoso/web uses a federated credential with subject repo:contoso/web:ref:refs/heads/main, so it deploys with no secrets stored.

lessons.title: Configuring API permissions
lessons.short: On the API permissions blade, add the delegated or application permissions your app needs from Microsoft Graph, other Microsoft APIs or your own APIs. Delegated permissions act for a signed-in user. Application permissions act as the app itself and always need admin consent. To publish your own scopes, use Expose an API.
lessons.deep:
**Requesting permissions**: App registration > **API permissions** > **Add a permission** > Microsoft APIs (Graph), **APIs my organization uses**, or **My APIs**.
- **Delegated permissions (scopes)**: the app acts **on behalf of a signed-in user**. Effective access is the overlap of the permission and the user's own rights. Some delegated permissions need admin consent (for example `Directory.Read.All`).
- **Application permissions (app roles)**: the app acts **as itself**, with no user, as in daemons and the client credentials flow. They **always require admin consent** and often grant tenant-wide access, such as `Mail.Read` for every mailbox.
- **Grant admin consent for <tenant>**: a button that consents tenant-wide. The Status column shows 'Granted for <tenant>'. CLI: `az ad app permission admin-consent --id <appId>`.
- Listing permissions on the registration is a request. The actual grants live on the service principal (Enterprise apps > Permissions).
**Exposing your own API**: on **Expose an API**, set the **Application ID URI** (default `api://<client-id>`), add **scopes** (delegated permissions such as `Orders.Read`, with 'Who can consent'), and optionally list **authorized client applications** that skip consent prompts. Application permissions for your API are defined as **app roles** with allowed member type Applications.
**Least privilege**: request the narrowest permission, such as `User.Read` rather than `User.Read.All`, and remove unused ones. In the client credentials flow, apps request `https://graph.microsoft.com/.default`.

terms.d: A delegated permission exposed by an API, such as Orders.Read.
The identifier of an exposed API, by default api://<client-id>.
A scope that requests all statically configured permissions of the app for a resource.

lessons.trap: For a background daemon with no signed-in user, delegated permissions are wrong. It needs application permissions plus admin consent.
lessons.example: A nightly export daemon gets the Graph application permission User.Read.All, and a Privileged Role Administrator grants admin consent for the tenant.

lessons.title: Creating app roles
lessons.short: App roles are custom roles you define on an app registration, such as Survey.Create. Assign them to users, groups or applications, and they appear in the token's roles claim. Each role has a display name, a value, a description, allowed member types (Users/Groups, Applications or both) and an enabled flag.
lessons.deep:
**Create**: App registration > **App roles** > **Create app role**:
- **Display name**: shown in assignment and consent screens, for example 'Survey Writer'.
- **Allowed member types**: **Users/Groups** (`User` in the manifest), **Applications** (`Application`), or **Both**.
- **Value**: the string in the `roles` claim, for example `Survey.Create`. It can't contain spaces and must match your code exactly.
- **Description**.
- **Do you want to enable this app role?** (`isEnabled`). You must disable a role before deleting it, and disabled roles still appear in existing tokens until assignments are removed.
**Assign**
- Users and groups: Enterprise apps > [app] > **Users and groups** > select a role.
- Applications: in the client app's **API permissions** > **My APIs** > choose the API > **Application permissions**, then **grant admin consent**. The role then appears in the client's access token.
**Tokens**: sign-in scenarios put roles in the **ID token**. App-calls-API scenarios put them in the **access token** issued for the API.
**App roles vs groups**: app roles are defined per app, travel with it across tenants, and are deleted with it. Groups are tenant objects and appear in the `groups` claim. Roles and exposed scopes share a default limit of 700 definitions per app.

terms.d: The manifest property defining whether a role is assignable to User, Application, or both.
A token claim listing the values of app roles assigned to the user or service principal.
Whether an app role can still be assigned; it must be false before you delete the role.

lessons.trap: If a role is created with Users/Groups only, it won't appear under Application permissions for a daemon client. You need Applications or Both.
lessons.example: The Orders API defines Orders.Process with allowedMemberTypes Application. The warehouse daemon is granted it as an application permission with admin consent.

lessons.title: Cloud discovery in Defender for Cloud Apps
lessons.short: Cloud discovery analyzes traffic logs from firewalls and proxies, or endpoint data from Defender for Endpoint, to find shadow IT: the cloud apps people really use. Snapshot reports come from manual uploads. Continuous reports come from a log collector, Defender for Endpoint, or secure web gateway integrations.
lessons.deep:
**Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps** is Microsoft's cloud access security broker (CASB). **Cloud discovery** compares traffic against the **cloud app catalog** (over 31,000 apps) and gives each app a risk score.
**Data sources**
- **Snapshot reports**: manually upload a firewall or proxy log for a one-time view.
- **Continuous reports**:
  - **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint integration**: built in. It covers devices on and off the corporate network and lets you investigate per machine.
  - **Log collector** (a Docker container) receives logs over Syslog or FTP from network appliances.
  - **Secure web gateway** integrations: Zscaler, iboss, Corrata, Menlo Security.
- The **Cloud Discovery API** automates log upload.
Data is analyzed several times a day. You can **anonymize** usernames in discovery data.
**Analyze**: the Cloud discovery dashboard shows top apps, users and IPs, app categories, risk levels and app headquarters locations. The **Discovered apps** tab supports filters (risk score, compliance, users, traffic).
**Govern**: tag apps **Sanctioned**, **Unsanctioned** or **Monitored**. With Defender for Endpoint and **Enforce app access** enabled, Unsanctioned apps are **blocked** and Monitored apps show a **warning** that users can bypass. Enforcement uses Defender Antivirus network protection in block mode. You can also generate **block scripts** for firewalls and proxies. **App discovery policies** alert on new risky apps or tag them automatically.

terms.d: Cloud apps used without IT's knowledge or approval.
A Docker-based component that receives firewall/proxy logs over Syslog or FTP for continuous reports.
Marks an app as not approved; with Defender for Endpoint it blocks access on devices.

lessons.trap: Snapshot reports are offered for ongoing monitoring with automatic anomaly detection. That needs continuous reports.
lessons.example: Contoso enables the Defender for Endpoint integration, finds 400 discovered apps, and tags a risky file-sharing site Unsanctioned. Defender for Endpoint then blocks it on laptops at home and in the office.

lessons.title: Connected apps (app connectors)
lessons.short: App connectors use a cloud provider's APIs to give Defender for Cloud Apps deep visibility into sanctioned apps such as Microsoft 365, Salesforce, Google Workspace, Box and AWS. They provide activities, files, accounts, OAuth app permissions and governance actions such as suspending users or quarantining files.
lessons.deep:
Cloud discovery shows which apps are used. **App connectors** go inside a sanctioned app through the vendor's **API**.
**Connect**: Microsoft Defender portal > **Settings** > **Cloud Apps** > **Connected apps** > **App Connectors** > **Connect an app**. Choose the app (for example Microsoft 365, Azure, AWS, GCP, Google Workspace, Salesforce, Box, Dropbox, Okta, ServiceNow, Slack, GitHub, Workday or Zendesk) and authorize with an **admin account** of that app (or OAuth or an API token).
**What a connector can provide** (it varies by app):
- **Account information**: users, groups, privileges.
- **Audit trail**: user, admin and sign-in activities for activity policies and anomaly detection.
- **Account governance**: suspend users, revoke sessions or passwords.
- **App permissions**: OAuth tokens granted by users (the basis for OAuth app policies).
- **Data scan and governance**: scan files and apply actions such as quarantine, removing sharing or applying labels.
Connectors work **after the fact, through APIs** (API-based CASB). **Conditional Access app control** works in **real time, inline**. They complement each other. Initial scans can take a long time because providers throttle API calls. Check connector status and fix errors on the Connected apps page.

terms.d: An API integration that gives Defender for Cloud Apps visibility and governance in a connected app.
Out-of-band inspection of activities and data through the app's APIs.
An automated response such as suspend user, quarantine file or remove external sharing.

lessons.trap: When the requirement is to scan files already stored in Box and quarantine them, Conditional Access app control is wrong. That needs an app connector.
lessons.example: After connecting Salesforce, the SOC sees admin activities and creates a policy that suspends any user who mass-exports reports.

lessons.title: Application-enforced restrictions
lessons.short: The 'Use app enforced restrictions' session control in Conditional Access passes device state to SharePoint Online, OneDrive and Exchange Online. Those apps then give unmanaged devices a limited, browser-only experience: no download, print or sync. You configure SharePoint with its unmanaged device access setting or Set-SPOTenant.
lessons.deep:
**What it is**: a **session control** in a Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policy. Entra ID sends device information (compliant or hybrid joined) to the cloud app, and the **app enforces** a full or limited experience. It's simpler than Conditional Access app control and needs no proxy, but only some Microsoft 365 apps support it.
**SharePoint Online and OneDrive**
- SharePoint admin center > **Policies** > **Access control** > **Unmanaged devices** > **Allow limited, web-only access**, or
- PowerShell: `Set-SPOTenant -ConditionalAccessPolicy AllowLimitedAccess` (other values: AllowFullAccess, BlockAccess). You can also set it per site with `Set-SPOSite`.
- This automatically creates Entra Conditional Access policies that use **Use app enforced restrictions**. Users on unmanaged devices can view files in the browser but can't download, print or sync them.
**Exchange Online**: Outlook on the web with `Set-OwaMailboxPolicy -ConditionalAccessPolicy ReadOnly` (attachments viewable in the browser, not downloadable), plus a CA policy that uses app enforced restrictions.
**Compare**: app-enforced restrictions mean full or limited, decided by the app. **Conditional Access app control** (Defender for Cloud Apps) gives fine-grained, content-aware session policies for many SaaS apps, such as blocking only downloads labeled Highly Confidential.

terms.d: A Conditional Access session control that lets supported apps limit the experience on unmanaged devices.
The SharePoint tenant setting that gives web-only, no-download access from unmanaged devices.
A device that is neither compliant (Intune) nor Microsoft Entra hybrid joined.

lessons.trap: App enforced restrictions work only for apps that support them, such as SharePoint, OneDrive and Exchange Online. For Salesforce or Box, use Conditional Access app control.
lessons.example: Contractors on personal laptops open SharePoint documents in the browser but see no Download or Sync buttons because AllowLimitedAccess is set.

lessons.title: Conditional Access app control
lessons.short: Conditional Access app control routes browser sessions through Defender for Cloud Apps so access and session policies run in real time. You enable it with the 'Use Conditional Access App Control' session control in an Entra Conditional Access policy. Edge gets in-browser protection, and other browsers are reverse-proxied with a .mcas.ms suffix.
lessons.deep:
**How it works**
1. Create a Microsoft Entra **Conditional Access** policy that targets users and apps. Under **Session**, select **Use Conditional Access App Control**.
2. When a user signs in, the session goes to Defender for Cloud Apps. **Microsoft Edge for Business** enforces policies **in the browser** (shown by a lock icon). Other browsers go through a **reverse proxy**, and URLs gain a suffix such as `contoso.my.salesforce.com.mcas.ms`.
3. Defender for Cloud Apps **access policies** and **session policies** decide what happens.
**Onboarding**: apps that use Entra ID for SAML or OIDC SSO onboard **automatically** after the first sign-in through a CA app control policy. Apps on non-Microsoft IdPs need manual onboarding. App Proxy apps are supported too, and they need Entra pre-authentication.
**Requirements**: Defender for Cloud Apps licence plus **Microsoft Entra ID P1**. It needs no agent on the device, so it suits unmanaged and BYOD devices.
**Limits**: session controls cover **browser** sessions. Native apps with non-interactive sign-in can't be proxied, so block them with an access policy that filters on Client app = Mobile and desktop. The Teams desktop app doesn't support session controls.
**Device identification**: Intune compliance, Entra hybrid join, or client certificates.

terms.d: Defender for Cloud Apps sits inline and rewrites app URLs (.mcas.ms) to inspect sessions.
Microsoft Edge for Business enforces session policies natively without URL redirection.
The Entra Conditional Access session control that hands sessions to Defender for Cloud Apps.

lessons.trap: Conditional Access app control is not set up only in the Defender portal. It starts with an Entra Conditional Access policy that uses the session control.
lessons.example: A CA policy for the Salesforce app selects Use Conditional Access App Control. Unmanaged-device users browsing Salesforce get the .mcas.ms suffix in Chrome and are monitored.

lessons.title: Access policies and session policies
lessons.short: With Conditional Access app control, an access policy decides at sign-in whether a session is allowed (Audit) or blocked (Block). A session policy lets the session continue and controls activity in it: Monitor only, Block activities, Control file download or Control file upload. Download control can Protect files by applying a sensitivity label.
lessons.deep:
Create both in the Defender portal > **Cloud Apps** > **Policies** > **Policy management** > **Conditional Access** > **Create policy**.
**Access policy**
- Filters: app, **client app** (browser or mobile and desktop), **device tags** (Intune compliant, Entra hybrid joined, valid client certificate), IP address, location, ISP, user and user agent.
- Actions: **Audit** (allow and log) or **Block** (with a custom user message).
- Example: block native desktop and mobile clients so users must use the browser, where session control applies.
**Session policy**: choose a **session control type**:
- **Monitor only**: logs sign-in activity.
- **Block activities**: for example block copy, cut, print, or sending a message that contains sensitive content.
- **Control file download (with inspection)**: actions **Audit**, **Block**, or **Protect** (applies a Microsoft Purview sensitivity label with encryption on download).
- **Control file upload (with inspection)**: for example block uploads of unlabeled files or malware.
- File filters include sensitivity label, name, extension and size. Content inspection can use Purview DLP.
- **Require step-up authentication** (authentication context) re-runs Conditional Access before a sensitive action.
When session policies conflict, the **more restrictive** action wins. Test with a test user and the Activity log (Source = Access control).

terms.d: A Defender for Cloud Apps policy that allows (audit) or blocks a session at sign-in based on conditions.
A real-time policy controlling actions inside an allowed session, like downloads or uploads.
Applies a sensitivity label (with encryption) to files as they are downloaded.

lessons.trap: When users on unmanaged devices must keep browsing but not download confidential files, an access policy is wrong because it blocks everything. Use a session policy with Control file download.
lessons.example: A session policy blocks downloads of files labeled Highly Confidential from SharePoint on unmanaged devices, while still allowing viewing in the browser.

lessons.title: OAuth app policies and app governance
lessons.short: Users can authorize third-party OAuth apps to read their mail, files or calendars. With app connectors in place, Defender for Cloud Apps lists these OAuth apps for Microsoft 365, Google Workspace and Salesforce, with permission level and community use. OAuth app policies alert on risky apps and can revoke them. App governance adds deeper policies and detections.
lessons.deep:
**OAuth apps page** (Cloud Apps > OAuth apps; moved to **App governance** when that is enabled):
- Columns and filters: **permission level** (High, Medium, Low), **community use** (Common, Uncommon, Rare), number of authorizing users, publisher and publisher verification, last authorized.
- Actions per app: **Approve** (marks it as reviewed, with no effect on users) or **Ban**, which disables the app. For Microsoft 365, banning disables the related enterprise app, and you can notify users who granted access.
**OAuth app policies** (Policy management > Create policy > OAuth app policy):
- Filters such as permission level = High, community use = Rare, or authorized by more than X users. Scope by the groups of the authorizing users.
- Governance actions include **revoke app** and **notify**. Built-in anomaly detections cover misleading publisher names and malicious OAuth apps.
**App governance** is included with a Defender for Cloud Apps licence and turned on in Settings > Cloud Apps > App governance. It provides insights, **app policies** (predefined and custom), threat detections and remediation for apps registered in Entra ID, Google and Salesforce. Its alerts show in Microsoft Defender XDR with detection source App Governance.
Prevention lives in Entra (user consent settings, admin consent workflow). Defender for Cloud Apps provides detection and response.

terms.d: A third-party app users authorize (via consent) to access their data through APIs.
How common an app is across Defender for Cloud Apps customers: common, uncommon or rare.
A Defender for Cloud Apps add-on capability for policies, insights and detections on OAuth apps.

lessons.trap: Banning an OAuth app in Defender for Cloud Apps isn't the same as the Entra user consent setting. Ban responds to existing grants, and consent settings prevent new ones.
lessons.example: An OAuth app policy alerts when a rare app requesting high permissions is authorized by more than 50 users, and revokes it automatically if an admin authorized it.

lessons.title: The cloud app catalog and risk scores
lessons.short: The cloud app catalog rates more than 31,000 cloud apps on over 90 risk factors in four categories: General, Security, Compliance and Legal. Scores run from 0 to 10, and higher is safer. You can adjust score weights, tag apps, request a score update, or suggest a missing app.
lessons.deep:
**Cloud app catalog** (Defender portal > **Cloud Apps** > **Cloud app catalog**):
- Holds **31,000+** apps, assessed by Microsoft analysts and automation.
- **90+ risk factors** in four categories:
  - **General**: company information such as founding year, domain age, popularity and headquarters.
  - **Security**: MFA support, encryption at rest, TLS version, admin audit trail, penetration testing.
  - **Compliance**: certifications such as ISO 27001, SOC 2, HIPAA and PCI DSS.
  - **Legal**: data ownership, data retention, GDPR readiness, DMCA.
- The **risk score** (0 to 10) is a weighted average of the category scores. A **higher score means lower risk**.
**Customizing**: Settings > Cloud Discovery > **Score metrics** lets you change the weight of categories and fields, or ignore some, so scores reflect your priorities.
**Using the catalog**
- Filter by category, risk score or compliance, and compare apps before sanctioning one.
- Tag apps **Sanctioned**, **Unsanctioned**, **Monitored** or a custom tag directly from the catalog, even before they're discovered.
- **Request score update** (the 'Suggest an improvement' dialog) when an attribute is wrong.
- **Suggest new app** from Discovered apps when an app isn't in the catalog. You can also add custom apps.

terms.d: Microsoft's database of 31,000+ cloud apps with risk assessments.
A 0–10 rating of an app (higher is safer), a weighted average of General, Security, Compliance and Legal.
Settings that let you change risk factor weights to fit your organization.

lessons.trap: A score of 9 isn't 'high risk'. In Defender for Cloud Apps, higher scores mean safer apps.
lessons.example: Before approving a new diagramming tool, an admin compares three catalog entries. They choose the one with a score of 9, SOC 2 and data-at-rest encryption, and tag it Sanctioned.

lessons.title: Planning entitlements
lessons.short: Entitlement management in Microsoft Entra ID Governance bundles groups, apps and SharePoint Online sites into **access packages** that users request, get approved for, and lose automatically when access expires.
lessons.deep:
Before building anything, map *who needs what, for how long, and who decides*. **Entitlement management** answers this with four building blocks:
- **Catalog**: a container of resources plus the people allowed to manage them.
- **Access package**: a bundle of resource roles (group membership, app role, SharePoint site role) from one catalog.
- **Policy**: who can request, the approval flow, and lifecycle (expiry, extension, access reviews). One package can have several policies, for example one for employees and one for partners.
- **Assignment**: a user holding the package; when it ends, access to every bundled resource is removed.

Planning steps: inventory resources, group them by job function or project, choose catalog owners close to the business, decide approvers and expiry, then decide whether external users from **connected organizations** may request.

Licensing: core entitlement management (requests, approvals, multi-stage approval, external user lifecycle) needs **Microsoft Entra ID P2** or **Microsoft Entra ID Governance**. Some newer features, such as **automatic assignment policies** and **custom extensions** (Logic Apps), need **ID Governance** specifically.

terms.d: Bundle of resource roles with policies that govern request, approval and expiry.
Rules in an access package: who can request, approvals, lifecycle.
A user's grant of an access package; removing it removes the bundled access.

lessons.trap: The exam expects you to pick entitlement management, not dynamic groups or manual group membership, when the requirement is request-plus-approval with automatic expiry.
lessons.example: A project team needs a Teams team, a SaaS app and a SharePoint site for six months; you put all three in one access package with a 180-day expiry.

lessons.title: Catalogs and delegated roles
lessons.short: A **catalog** groups resources and access packages and defines who can manage them. Delegate with catalog roles such as **Catalog owner**, **Access package manager** and **Access package assignment manager** instead of handing out directory admin roles.
lessons.deep:
Every access package lives in exactly one catalog, and a package **cannot be moved** to another catalog later. A built-in **General** catalog exists by default.

Resources you can add: cloud-created **Microsoft 365 groups** and **security groups** (and therefore Teams), **enterprise applications**, and **SharePoint Online sites**. You **cannot** add on-premises AD synced groups or Exchange Online distribution groups.

Delegation roles (entitlement-management-specific):
- **Catalog creator** (tenant-wide): creates catalogs and becomes their first owner.
- **Catalog owner**: manages resources, packages and roles in the catalog.
- **Catalog reader**: views packages in the catalog.
- **Access package manager**: creates and edits packages from resources already in the catalog.
- **Access package assignment manager**: assigns/removes users and manages requests, but cannot create or edit packages.

The least-privileged directory role for all entitlement tasks is **Identity Governance Administrator**. To add a resource, a non-admin catalog owner must also own that group or app. The catalog setting **Enabled for external users** must be **Yes** before connected-organization users can request its packages.

terms.d: Manages a catalog's resources, packages and delegated roles.
Can assign users and handle requests but not edit packages.
Catalog switch that lets connected-organization users request its packages.

lessons.trap: Access package managers cannot add new resources to the catalog; only catalog owners (who also own the resource) or admins can.
lessons.example: HR's catalog owner adds the HR SharePoint site and delegates Access package assignment manager to a help-desk lead who only adds and removes people.

lessons.title: Access packages: resources and request policies
lessons.short: An access package lists **resource roles** and at least one **policy**. The policy's *Who can get access* is **For users in your directory**, **For users not in your directory**, or **None (administrator direct assignments only)**.
lessons.deep:
Creating a package (ID Governance > Entitlement management > Access packages > New): Basics (name, catalog), **Resource roles** (for example *Member* of a group or a specific app role), **Requests**, **Requestor information**, **Lifecycle**.

Request policy scopes:
- **For users in your directory**: specific users and groups, all members (excluding guests), or all users including guests.
- **For users not in your directory**: specific connected organizations, all configured connected organizations, or **All users** (any external identity).
- **None (administrator direct assignments only)**: nobody requests; managers assign.

Approval settings: require approval, require requestor justification, **1 to 3 approval stages** (one approver per stage is enough), approvers can be the manager, sponsors, or specific users, with **fallback approvers** and alternate approvers if the first stage does not decide.

**Requestor information** adds questions (short text, multiple choice, long text) shown to approvers. Setting **Hidden = Yes** removes the package from browsing in My Access but anyone with the direct link can still request. Adding a resource to an existing package grants it to everyone already assigned.

terms.d: The permission granted by a resource, e.g. group Member or an app role.
One step of up to three in an approval workflow; any one approver in the stage can decide.
Package does not appear in My Access search but is requestable by link.

lessons.trap: Hidden does not block requests; only the policy's scope controls who can request.
lessons.example: Sales contractors get a package with a two-stage approval: their sponsor, then the sales director.

lessons.title: Access packages: lifecycle, separation of duties and auto-assignment
lessons.short: Lifecycle settings set when assignments **expire** (on a date, after days/hours, or never), whether users can **extend**, and whether **access reviews** recur. **Separation of duties** blocks requests from users holding incompatible packages or groups.
lessons.deep:
**Lifecycle**: assignments can expire on a specific date, after a number of days (0 to 3660) or hours, or never. *Users can request specific timeline* lets requestors choose start and end dates. *Allow users to extend access* sends reminders before expiry and can require approval for the extension. *Require access reviews* schedules recurring reviews of the package's assignments.

**Separation of duties**: on a package's *Separation of duties* page you list **incompatible access packages** and **incompatible groups**. A user who already holds one cannot request (and an admin cannot newly assign) the package. Rules are **one-directional**, so configure both packages to block both ways. Existing overlapping assignments are not removed; the *Additional access* column shows them.

**Automatic assignment policy**: assigns the package to users matching an attribute rule (for example `user.department -eq "Sales"`) and removes it when they stop matching. Requires **Microsoft Entra ID Governance**.

**Custom extensions** call Azure Logic Apps at stages like request created or assignment granted, also an ID Governance feature.

terms.d: Incompatible packages or groups that block a request.
Rule-based policy that assigns and removes a package by user attributes.
Logic Apps workflow triggered by entitlement management events.

lessons.trap: Candidates assume incompatibility is two-way or removes existing access; it is one-way and only blocks new requests and assignments.
lessons.example: Users with the Development environment package are blocked from requesting Production environment until their Dev assignment is removed.

lessons.title: Managing access requests
lessons.short: Users request packages in the **My Access** portal (myaccess.microsoft.com). Requests move through states such as **Pending approval**, **Delivering**, **Delivered**, **Denied** and **Expired**, and admins can view, reprocess or remove them.
lessons.deep:
Request flow: a user signs in to **https://myaccess.microsoft.com**, finds a package (or uses its direct link), answers questions and gives justification. If approval is needed the request is **Pending approval** and approvers get email linking to My Access *Approvals*. Outcomes:
- **Denied**: an approver rejected it.
- **Expired**: no approver decided before the deadline; the user must resubmit.
- **Delivering / Partially delivered**: provisioning to resources is in progress or incomplete.
- **Delivered**: access to all resources is in place.

Admins (Identity Governance Administrator, Catalog owner, Access package manager or Access package assignment manager) open the package's **Requests** page to see details and **Request history** (who approved, justifications, delivery time). Requests in **Partially delivered** or failed states can be **reprocessed**. **Remove** on a completed request deletes only the record; the user's assignment remains, so remove the *assignment* to revoke access.

Approvers can be forwarded to **alternate approvers** after a number of days; multi-stage requests need each stage to approve. Admin direct assignments skip the request process and do not send request completion emails.

terms.d: End-user portal for requesting packages and doing approvals and reviews.
Retry delivery for a partially delivered or failed request.
A request no approver acted on in time; must be resubmitted.

lessons.trap: Removing a request record does not remove access; you must remove the assignment.
lessons.example: A new hire's request shows Partially delivered because a SharePoint site failed; the access package manager reprocesses it.

lessons.title: Terms of use (ToU)
lessons.short: **Terms of use** policies show a PDF that users must accept before access is granted. They are enforced by a **Conditional Access** grant control and need **Microsoft Entra ID P1**.
lessons.deep:
Create ToU in Entra admin center under Conditional Access > **Terms of use** (Conditional Access Administrator). Settings:
- **PDF document**, one per language; users see the version matching their browser language.
- **Require users to expand the terms of use** before accepting.
- **Require users to consent on every device**: users must accept on each device, which must be registered in Entra ID. Not supported for B2B guests or the Intune Enrollment app.
- **Expire consents** (start date plus frequency) or **Duration before re-acceptance required (days)** for per-user cycles.

Enforcement: add the ToU as a **Grant** control in a Conditional Access policy targeting users and apps (exclude service accounts). Declining blocks access. A tenant can have up to **40** terms of use.

Editing: you cannot change an uploaded document; upload a **new version** and optionally select **Require reaccept**. Reporting: the Terms of use page shows **Accepted/Declined** counts (Security Reader can view), and each acceptance writes an **audit log** event. Users can review terms they accepted in **My Account**. A common pattern is a Conditional Access policy that targets **guest or external users** so partners accept an agreement before reaching shared resources.

terms.d: PDF agreement users accept before access, enforced by Conditional Access.
Forces acceptance of a newly uploaded version at next access.
Per-device acceptance; needs Entra-registered devices.

lessons.trap: ToU is enforced with a Conditional Access grant control, not a session control or an Intune compliance policy.
lessons.example: Guests must accept an NDA before reaching the partner SharePoint site; a CA policy targeting guest users grants access only after ToU acceptance.

lessons.title: Lifecycle of external users
lessons.short: Guests invited through entitlement management can be **blocked from signing in** and then **removed** when their last access package assignment ends. By default they are blocked, then deleted after **30 days**.
lessons.deep:
When an external user requests a package via a policy *For users not in your directory* and is approved, entitlement management invites them as a B2B guest. Tenant-wide settings under **Entitlement management > Settings** (Lifecycle of external users) decide what happens when their **last** assignment expires or is removed:
- **Block external user from signing in to this directory**: Yes/No.
- **Remove external user**: Yes/No.
- **Number of days before removing external user from this directory**: default **30**; **0** removes immediately.

Important behaviour:
- Only guests invited by entitlement management (or marked as **governed**) are affected; guests who already existed are left alone.
- A blocked user cannot request new packages, so don't block if they may need access again.
- Changes apply to users losing their last assignment after the change.

Pair this with **access reviews of guests** and access package expiry so guest accounts don't linger. The capability to **mark an existing guest as governed** needs Microsoft Entra ID Governance.

terms.d: External user whose lifecycle is managed by entitlement management.
The trigger: lifecycle actions fire only when no package assignments remain.
Grace period (default 30) between blocking and deleting the guest.

lessons.trap: Lifecycle actions fire when the user's last assignment ends, not when any single assignment ends, and they don't touch pre-existing guests.
lessons.example: A contractor's only package expires on 30 June; they're blocked that day and their guest object is deleted 30 days later.

lessons.title: Connected organizations
lessons.short: A **connected organization** is a partner directory or domain whose users may request access packages. States are **Configured** (admin-created, fully functional) or **Proposed** (auto-created when an unknown external user requests).
lessons.deep:
Create one under Entitlement management > **Connected organizations**, by pointing at another **Microsoft Entra tenant**, a **domain** (for SAML/WS-Fed federation or email one-time passcode users), or a Microsoft account. Add **sponsors**: **internal sponsors** are members of your directory; **external sponsors** are guests from that organization already in your directory. Sponsors can be used as approvers in package policies.

**States**:
- **Configured**: in scope for policies targeting *All configured connected organizations*.
- **Proposed**: created automatically when someone from an unknown domain requests a package whose policy allows **All users**. Proposed orgs are **not** included in *all configured connected organizations* policies; change the state to Configured to include them.

The **Connected Organization Administrator** role manages connected organizations. A policy scoped to *All users* also requires **email one-time passcode** to be enabled and must not conflict with B2B allow/block lists, which take precedence. Delete a connected organization when the partnership ends.

terms.d: External directory or domain allowed to request access packages.
Auto-created connected org, not covered by 'all configured' policies.
Guest from the partner org who can approve its users' requests.

lessons.trap: A Proposed connected organization's users are not covered by a policy for 'all configured connected organizations'.
lessons.example: Fabrikam is added as a configured connected organization with its project lead as an external sponsor who approves Fabrikam requests.

lessons.title: Planning access reviews
lessons.short: **Access reviews** let owners, managers, users themselves or chosen reviewers recertify who still needs **group membership**, **app assignments**, **access package assignments**, **Entra roles** or **Azure resource roles**, on a recurring schedule.
lessons.deep:
Planning questions: *what* to review, *who* reviews, *how often*, and *what happens* to unanswered or denied users.

Where each review is created:
- Groups (security and Microsoft 365, including Teams) and enterprise apps: **ID Governance > Access reviews**.
- Access package assignments: inside the access package lifecycle settings (entitlement management).
- Entra roles and Azure resource roles: **Privileged Identity Management > Access reviews**.

Reviewer choices: **group owners**, **selected users or groups**, **users review their own access** (self-review), **managers of users**, with **fallback reviewers** where no manager/owner exists. **Multi-stage reviews** (up to three stages) chain reviewers, for example self-review then manager.

Licensing: access reviews are a governance feature (Microsoft Entra ID P2 or ID Governance); reviews scoped to **inactive users only** and **user-to-group affiliation** (machine-learning) recommendations need **Microsoft Entra ID Governance**. Creating group/app reviews needs at least **Identity Governance Administrator**; group owners can create them only if the tenant setting *Group owners can create and manage access reviews for groups they own* is **Yes** (default No). PIM role reviews need Privileged Role Administrator.

terms.d: Periodic recertification of who should keep access.
Reviewer used when the user has no manager or the group has no owner.
Up to three sequential reviewer stages in one review.

lessons.trap: Entra role and Azure role reviews are created from PIM, not from the generic Access reviews blade's group/app wizard.
lessons.example: Quarterly, each manager reviews their reports' access to the finance app; users with no manager go to the finance lead as fallback.

lessons.title: Creating and configuring access reviews
lessons.short: A review defines **scope** (Everyone, **Guest users only**, or **Inactive users** for 1–730 days), **reviewers**, **recurrence and duration**, **upon completion** behaviour and **decision helpers**.
lessons.deep:
Key settings in the wizard:
- **Scope**: *Teams + Groups* or *Applications*; choose *Select Teams + groups* or *All Microsoft 365 groups with guest users* (guest-only scope). User scope: *Everyone*, *Guest users only*, or *Inactive users (tenant level)* with **Days inactive 1–730**.
- **Reviewers** and optional multi-stage settings.
- **Recurrence**: one time, weekly, monthly, quarterly, semi-annually, annually; the **duration** must fit inside the recurrence interval (weekly allows up to 7 days).
- **Upon completion**: **Auto apply results to resource**; **If reviewers don't respond**: *No change*, *Remove access*, *Approve access* or *Take recommendations*; **Action to apply on denied guest users**: *Remove user's membership from the resource* or *Block user from signing in for 30 days, then remove user from the tenant*.
- **Decision helpers**: *No sign-in within 30 days* and *User-to-Group Affiliation*.
- **Advanced**: justification required, email notifications, **reminders** (sent at the midpoint), additional email content.

Reviews take a **snapshot** at start; nested group members are reviewed individually. Graph: `POST /identityGovernance/accessReviews/definitions`; PowerShell `New-MgIdentityGovernanceAccessReviewDefinition`.

terms.d: Automatically removes denied access when the review ends.
Applies system recommendations to users reviewers ignored.
Recommendation signal such as no sign-in within 30 days.

lessons.trap: Combining 'Remove access' or 'Take recommendations' with auto-apply can strip access from users nobody reviewed; know which option leaves access unchanged (No change).
lessons.example: A monthly review of guests in all Microsoft 365 groups blocks denied guests for 30 days and then deletes them.

lessons.title: Monitoring access review activity
lessons.short: Admins track reviews on each review's **Overview** and **Results** pages, download decisions as **CSV**, build **Review History** reports, and query audit events in Log Analytics or workbooks.
lessons.deep:
In **ID Governance > Access reviews**, each review series shows the **current instance**: progress (reviewed vs not reviewed), status (for example *In progress*, *Completed*, *Applying*, *Result applied*) and per-user decisions on **Results**, with reviewer, decision and justification. Select **Download** for a UTF-8 **CSV** of an in-progress or completed instance.

**Review History** (Access reviews > Review History > New report) produces a downloadable CSV across many reviews filtered by date range, review type (group, application, Entra role, Azure role, access package) and result (Approve, Deny, Not reviewed). Reports stay downloadable for **30 days**.

For long-term analysis, send **audit logs** to a Log Analytics workspace with diagnostic settings; review events appear in `AuditLogs` (for example `LoggedByService == "Access Reviews"`). Workbooks can chart the data. Programmatically, list decisions with Graph `accessReviewInstance: listDecisions` or `Get-MgIdentityGovernanceAccessReviewDefinitionInstanceDecision`.

Reviewers receive a start email and an automatic **reminder** halfway through; admins can send reminders and watch for low completion before the end date.

terms.d: Report builder that exports review decisions across reviews to CSV.
Per-user decisions for the current review instance.
The active occurrence of a recurring review series.

lessons.trap: The Review History report is kept for 30 days; for longer retention route audit logs to Log Analytics or storage.
lessons.example: Before the quarterly SOX audit, the identity team generates a Review History report of all application reviews for the last year.

lessons.title: Manually responding to access reviews
lessons.short: Reviewers decide **Approve**, **Deny** or **Don't know** in **My Access**, can **Accept recommendations**, and may change decisions until the review ends. Admins can **Stop** a review early and **Apply** results manually.
lessons.deep:
Reviewers open the **Start review** email link or **https://myaccess.microsoft.com** > Access reviews. For each user: **Approve**, **Deny**, or **Don't know** (user keeps access; decision is recorded). A **Reason** is required if the admin enabled justification. **Accept recommendations** applies the decision helpers to selected or all unreviewed users. Decisions can be changed any time before the review ends; with several reviewers the **last submitted** response counts. Denied users are not removed until the review ends or is stopped.

Admin actions on an instance:
- **Stop**: end early; reviewers can no longer respond and a stopped review **can't be restarted**.
- **Apply**: if *Auto apply results* was off, open **Series > Review history**, choose the instance and select Apply; denied users are removed within minutes.
- **Stop current stage**: in a multi-stage review, move to the next stage.
- Send reminders and **Reset** decisions where needed.

Applying cannot remove users from **on-premises synced groups** or **dynamic groups**, or users who get access via a nested group; those need manual action at the source.

terms.d: Reviewer decision that keeps the user's access and logs the choice.
Ends a review instance early; it cannot be restarted.
Manually enforces denials when auto-apply is disabled.

lessons.trap: Denials are not enforced until the review ends or is stopped, and only applied if auto-apply is on or an admin selects Apply.
lessons.example: The finance review finished with auto-apply disabled; the admin opens Review history and applies results, removing 12 denied users.

lessons.title: PIM for Microsoft Entra roles: assignments
lessons.short: **Privileged Identity Management (PIM)** gives just-in-time admin access. An **eligible** assignment must be activated before use; an **active** assignment always applies. Either can be **permanent** or **time-bound**.
lessons.deep:
PIM is part of Microsoft Entra ID Governance and needs **Microsoft Entra ID P2** or **ID Governance** for users with eligible or time-bound assignments. Assign at **ID Governance > Privileged Identity Management > Microsoft Entra roles > Roles > Add assignments** as at least **Privileged Role Administrator**.

Assignment types:
- **Eligible**: the user activates in PIM (**My roles**), possibly with MFA, justification or approval.
- **Active**: always on, no activation needed.
- Durations: **permanent** or **time-bound** (start and end date).

Scope can be the whole directory or, for supported roles, an **administrative unit** or a single application. You can assign roles to users, **role-assignable groups** and agent identities.

Rules worth knowing: an assignment can't be shorter than **5 minutes** or removed within 5 minutes of creation; PIM never automatically removes the **last Global Administrator** assignment. Users can request **extend** (within 14 days of expiry) or **renew** (up to 30 days after expiry), which admins approve. Graph: eligible assignment via `roleEligibilityScheduleRequests` with `action: adminAssign`; user activation via `roleAssignmentScheduleRequests` with `action: selfActivate`.

terms.d: Role a user must activate before using.
Role that is always in effect without activation.
Assignment with start and end date, e.g. for contractors.

lessons.trap: Eligible means 'can activate', not 'has the permissions now'; the exam often asks which type requires activation.
lessons.example: Helpdesk staff get an eligible, time-bound User Administrator assignment for 6 months and activate it only when needed.

lessons.title: PIM for Microsoft Entra roles: role settings
lessons.short: Each role's **settings** control activation: **maximum duration (1–24 hours)**, **MFA** or **Conditional Access authentication context**, justification, ticket information, **approval**, assignment expiration rules and notifications.
lessons.deep:
Open PIM > Microsoft Entra roles > **Settings** > select a role > **Edit**. Tabs:
- **Activation**: *Activation maximum duration* (1–24 h); *On activation, require* **Azure MFA** or a **Microsoft Entra Conditional Access authentication context** (for authentication strengths or compliant devices); *Require justification*; *Require ticket information* (not validated against any system); *Require approval to activate* with selected approvers.
- **Assignment**: *Allow permanent eligible assignment* or *Expire eligible assignments after* a period; same for active assignments; *Require MFA on active assignment*; *Require justification on active assignment*.
- **Notification**: emails for eligible/active assignments and activations, with default recipients, extra recipients and *critical emails only*.

If approval is required but **no approvers are specified**, **Privileged Role Administrators** and **Global Administrators** become default approvers. For authentication context, create and enable the Conditional Access policy first; if no enabled policy targets the context, PIM falls back to MFA. Settings are per role; in Graph they're **roleManagementPolicies** rules.

terms.d: How long an activation lasts, 1 to 24 hours.
Tag that links PIM activation to a Conditional Access policy.
Free-text ticket number recorded at activation; not validated.

lessons.trap: Settings are configured per role, not once for all roles, and the ticket field is never validated against ServiceNow or any ITSM tool.
lessons.example: Global Administrator activation is limited to 2 hours and requires approval from two named security leads plus a phishing-resistant authentication context.

lessons.title: PIM for Azure resources
lessons.short: PIM also governs **Azure RBAC roles** (Owner, Contributor, User Access Administrator, etc.) at **management group, subscription, resource group or resource** scope, with the same eligible/active model and per-role, per-scope settings.
lessons.deep:
Go to PIM > **Azure resources**. The current experience manages Azure resources without manual onboarding; in the legacy experience you **discover** a management group or subscription first. Bringing a resource under management creates the **MS-PIM** service principal with **User Access Administrator** on it, and a managed management group or subscription can't be unmanaged.

Who manages: **Owner** or **User Access Administrator** of the resource manages its PIM role settings and assignments (Global Administrators without access can **elevate access** first).

Key behaviours:
- **Role assignments** follow Azure RBAC inheritance: eligible Contributor on a subscription applies to its resource groups once activated.
- **Role settings** are per role and per scope and are **not inherited**: settings on a subscription don't flow to a resource group.
- Activation maximum duration is 1–24 hours; MFA, authentication context, justification, ticket and approval options match Entra roles.
- Unlike Entra roles, Azure resource roles have **no default approvers**; you must select at least one when requiring approval.
- Assignments can include **conditions** for some roles, and access reviews of Azure roles are created in PIM.

terms.d: Service principal PIM uses to manage Azure role assignments.
Management group, subscription, resource group or resource.
Lets a Global Administrator gain User Access Administrator at root scope.

lessons.trap: Role settings do not inherit down the Azure hierarchy even though role assignments do.
lessons.example: Developers get eligible Contributor on the production resource group, activated for up to 4 hours with approval by the platform lead.

lessons.title: PIM for Groups
lessons.short: **PIM for Groups** gives just-in-time **membership** or **ownership** of a security group or Microsoft 365 group. Each has its own activation policy. Dynamic groups and on-premises synced groups aren't supported.
lessons.deep:
PIM for Groups (formerly *Privileged Access Groups*) applies JIT to anything the group grants: app access, Azure roles, or Entra roles if the group is **role-assignable**.

Facts to know:
- Supported: **Microsoft Entra security groups** and **Microsoft 365 groups**. Not supported: **dynamic membership groups** and groups **synchronized from on-premises**.
- The group doesn't have to be role-assignable to be used with PIM; it must be role-assignable only to receive Entra role assignments (limit 500 role-assignable groups per tenant).
- Two separate roles and settings: **Member** and **Owner**, each with activation duration, MFA/authentication context, justification and approval.
- Assign under PIM > **Groups** > group > **Assignments** > Add assignments, choose Member or Owner, then Eligible or Active.
- Who can assign: for role-assignable groups, Privileged Role Administrator, Global Administrator or an active owner; for other groups, Groups Administrator, Identity Governance Administrator or an active owner.
- Every eligible member/owner needs **Entra ID P2** or **ID Governance**.
- For groups that elevate into Entra roles, Microsoft recommends **requiring approval** on eligible member activation.
- Group membership changes made outside PIM override PIM.

terms.d: Just-in-time membership or ownership of a group.
Group created with isAssignableToRole so it can hold Entra roles.
Two separately governed PIM roles on a group.

lessons.trap: Dynamic and on-premises synced groups can't be used with PIM for Groups; the group doesn't need to be role-assignable unless it will hold Entra roles.
lessons.example: The SQL-Admins security group grants Azure roles on database servers; DBAs are eligible members and activate for 3 hours.

lessons.title: PIM request and approval process
lessons.short: Eligible users activate in **My roles**; if approval is required the request goes to approvers on **Approve requests**. Approvers have **24 hours**, the **first** approver's decision wins, and nobody can approve their own request.
lessons.deep:
Activation flow: user opens PIM > **My roles** > Eligible assignments > **Activate**, enters duration (up to the maximum), justification, ticket, satisfies MFA or the authentication context, and submits. Without approval, the role activates within moments; with approval the request is **pending**.

Approvers receive email and open **PIM > Approve requests**, review the request and justification, add their own justification and **Approve** or **Deny**.

Rules:
- Approvers have **24 hours** to act; after that the user must submit a new request (not configurable).
- With several approvers, the **first approve or deny** resolves the request and everyone is notified.
- **Approvers can't approve their own** activation, and service principals can't approve.
- Global Administrators and Privileged Role Administrators can view and cancel pending requests; requesters can cancel their own pending requests.
- Users can **deactivate** early when finished; activations end automatically at the chosen duration.
- Extend/renew requests also go to administrators for approval.

Approval is configured per role in role settings; approvers can be users or groups.

terms.d: PIM page where users see and activate eligible assignments.
PIM page where approvers act on pending activations.
Ending an activation before its scheduled end.

lessons.trap: Requests are not approved by majority vote; the first approver to respond decides, and pending requests expire after 24 hours.
lessons.example: An engineer requests Exchange Administrator at 22:00; the on-call approver approves via the email link and the engineer activates for 2 hours.

lessons.title: PIM audit history, alerts and reports
lessons.short: PIM **Resource audit** shows all role activity for the last **30 days**; **My audit** shows your own. PIM **alerts** flag risky configuration such as roles assigned outside PIM. Keep longer history by routing audit logs to Log Analytics.
lessons.deep:
Audit: PIM > Microsoft Entra roles > **Resource audit** (all assignments, activations and policy changes; needs a role such as Privileged Role Administrator, Security Reader or Global Reader) or **My audit** (any user, own activity). Data covers the past **30 days**; for longer, use **diagnostic settings** to send `AuditLogs` to Log Analytics or a storage account, then query, for example, `AuditLogs | where OperationName has "Add member to role"`. Link related events with **roleAssignmentRequestId**.

Alerts (PIM > Microsoft Entra roles > **Alerts**; configure in Alerts > Settings as Privileged Role Administrator):
- **Roles are assigned outside PIM** (High)
- **Potential stale accounts in a privileged role** (Medium)
- **Administrators aren't using their privileged roles** (Low)
- **Roles don't require MFA for activation** (Low)
- **Too many Global Administrators** (Low; both a count and a percentage threshold must be met)
- **Roles are activated too frequently** (Low)
- **Organization doesn't have Entra ID P2 or ID Governance** (Low)

Azure resources and groups each have their own audit history in PIM. Pair alerts with **access reviews** of privileged roles.

terms.d: All PIM activity for a role type, last 30 days.
A user's own PIM activity.
Warning about risky privileged configuration, e.g. roles assigned outside PIM.

lessons.trap: PIM audit in the portal is 30 days; the fix for longer retention is diagnostic settings, not changing a PIM setting.
lessons.example: A High alert shows Global Administrator was assigned directly in Roles & admins; the admin converts it to an eligible PIM assignment.

lessons.title: Emergency access accounts
lessons.short: Keep **two or more** cloud-only **emergency access (break-glass)** accounts on the `*.onmicrosoft.com` domain with **permanent active Global Administrator**, phishing-resistant authentication, Conditional Access exclusions, and sign-in alerts.
lessons.deep:
Emergency access accounts prevent tenant lockout when federation, MFA, Conditional Access or admins are unavailable. Microsoft guidance:
- **Two or more** accounts, **cloud-only**, on the **\*.onmicrosoft.com** domain; not federated or synchronized from on-premises; not tied to one person or phone.
- Assign **Global Administrator** as a **permanent active** assignment in PIM (not eligible).
- Use a **phishing-resistant, passwordless** method that satisfies **mandatory MFA**, such as **passkeys (FIDO2)** (or certificate-based authentication if you run PKI), and preferably a different method from regular admins.
- **Exclude** them (via a dedicated group) from Conditional Access policies that block or restrict sign-in; report-only policies need no exclusion.
- Store credentials securely in separate locations, e.g. fireproof safes.
- **Monitor**: send sign-in logs to Log Analytics and create an alert rule on `SigninLogs` filtered on the accounts' **Object IDs** (UserId), threshold greater than 0, Severity 0 (Critical), with an action group.
- **Validate at least every 90 days** and after staff or licensing changes.

terms.d: Emergency access account used only when normal admin access fails.
Assignment that never expires and needs no activation.
Azure Monitor notification target (email, SMS) for alerts.

lessons.trap: Break-glass accounts should be permanent active, not eligible, and cloud-only, not synchronized from AD DS.
lessons.example: An alert fires when breakglass2@contoso.onmicrosoft.com signs in; the security team confirms it was the quarterly test.

lessons.title: Sign-in and audit logs
lessons.short: **Sign-in logs** record authentication events (interactive user, non-interactive user, service principal, managed identity). **Audit logs** record changes to users, groups, apps, roles and policies. Both are kept **7 days** on Free and **30 days** on P1/P2.
lessons.deep:
Find them in **Entra admin center > Entra ID > Monitoring & health**. Reading needs at least **Reports Reader** (Security Reader and Global Reader also work).

**Sign-in logs** tabs:
- **Interactive user sign-ins**: user provides a credential or completes MFA.
- **Non-interactive user sign-ins**: a client signs in on the user's behalf with a token (often aggregated).
- **Service principal sign-ins**: apps using secrets or certificates.
- **Managed identity sign-ins**: Azure-managed secrets.
Each entry has basic info, location, device, **Authentication details**, **Conditional Access** (which policies applied and their result) and **Report-only** tabs. Failure codes such as 50126 (invalid credentials) or 53003 (blocked by Conditional Access) help troubleshooting.

**Audit logs** show **Activity**, **Category** (e.g. UserManagement, RoleManagement), **Service**, initiator, target and result. They are system-generated and can't be edited.

Retention: audit and sign-in logs **7 days** (Free) or **30 days** (P1/P2). Upgrading doesn't recover older data, so route logs to Log Analytics or storage for longer retention.

terms.d: User presents a credential or MFA directly.
Token-based sign-in performed by a client for the user.
Record of directory changes and who made them.

lessons.trap: Service principal and managed identity sign-ins are separate tabs; a user's token refreshes are non-interactive, not service principal sign-ins.
lessons.example: A user says they're blocked; the sign-in log's Conditional Access tab shows a device compliance policy failed.

lessons.title: Provisioning logs
lessons.short: **Provisioning logs** show what the Microsoft Entra provisioning service did when creating, updating, disabling or deleting accounts in connected apps (SCIM, Workday, ServiceNow), with status **Success, Failure, Skipped or Warning**.
lessons.deep:
Open **Entra ID > Monitoring & health > Provisioning logs**, or from an enterprise app's **Provisioning** blade. Each event lists the **Identity**, **Action** (Create, Update, Delete, Disable, StagedDelete, Other), **Source system**, **Target system** and **Status**:
- **Success**: change applied.
- **Failure**: error; see **Troubleshooting & Recommendations** for the error code and fix.
- **Skipped**: user wasn't processed, often because they're **out of scope** (not assigned, or a scoping filter excluded them).
- **Warning**: completed with issues.

The detail pane has **Steps** (import, match, scope evaluation, provision), **Troubleshooting & Recommendations**, **Modified properties** (old/new values) and **Summary**. You can filter by identity, action, status, date and job and download records.

For trend analysis, stream **ProvisioningLogs** with diagnostic settings to Log Analytics and use the **Provisioning Analysis** workbook. Provisioning logs complement audit logs: audit shows configuration changes to the provisioning job, provisioning logs show per-object results.

terms.d: Entra engine that syncs accounts to apps, often via SCIM.
Status for objects not processed, commonly out of scope.
Before/after attribute values for a provisioning event.

lessons.trap: A user missing from a target app with status Skipped usually isn't assigned or is filtered out, not failing authentication.
lessons.example: Provisioning to ServiceNow shows Failure for one user; the Troubleshooting tab reports a duplicate email in the target.

lessons.title: Diagnostic settings and destinations
lessons.short: **Diagnostic settings** stream Entra logs to a **Log Analytics workspace** (query, alert, workbooks), a **storage account** (cheap long-term archive), an **event hub** (third-party SIEM) or a partner solution. Configuring them needs **Security Administrator**.
lessons.deep:
Path: **Entra ID > Monitoring & health > Diagnostic settings > Add diagnostic setting**. Choose log categories and one or more destinations; create multiple settings to send different categories to different places. The destination must already exist in an Azure subscription.

Common categories: **AuditLogs**, **SignInLogs**, **NonInteractiveUserSignInLogs**, **ServicePrincipalSignInLogs**, **ManagedIdentitySignInLogs**, **ProvisioningLogs**, **ADFSSignInLogs**, **RiskyUsers**, **UserRiskEvents**, **RiskyServicePrincipals**, **ServicePrincipalRiskEvents**, **MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs**, **NetworkAccessTrafficLogs**. Custom security attribute audit logs are configured separately and need **Attribute Log Administrator**.

Choosing a destination:
- **Log Analytics** (Azure Monitor Logs): regular KQL querying, **alert rules**, workbooks; the base for **Microsoft Sentinel**.
- **Storage account**: retain logs well beyond 30 days for compliance with rare access.
- **Event Hubs**: stream to a non-Microsoft SIEM such as Splunk or QRadar.
- **Partner solution**: Azure Native ISV services.

All destinations incur Azure costs. Data appears after a short delay, not instantly.

terms.d: Rule that routes chosen log categories to destinations.
Streaming endpoint used to feed external SIEMs.
Azure Monitor store for KQL queries, alerts and workbooks.

lessons.trap: Pick Event Hubs for third-party SIEM streaming, storage for cheap archive, Log Analytics for querying and alerts.
lessons.example: Contoso keeps two years of audit logs in a storage account for auditors and sends sign-in logs to Log Analytics for alerts.

lessons.title: Monitoring Entra ID with KQL
lessons.short: Once logs reach Log Analytics, query tables such as **SigninLogs**, **AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs**, **AuditLogs** and **AADProvisioningLogs** with **KQL** (`where`, `summarize`, `project`, `extend`, `ago()`, `bin()`), and turn queries into alert rules.
lessons.deep:
Open **Entra ID > Monitoring & health > Log Analytics** or the workspace in Azure Monitor. Main tables: `SigninLogs` (interactive), `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs`, `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`, `AADManagedIdentitySignInLogs`, `AuditLogs`, `AADProvisioningLogs`, `AADRiskyUsers`, `AADUserRiskEvents`, `MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs`.

Useful columns: SigninLogs has `UserPrincipalName`, `UserId`, `AppDisplayName`, `IPAddress`, `ResultType` (a string; "0" means success), `ConditionalAccessStatus` (success, failure, notApplied), `AuthenticationRequirement`, `ClientAppUsed`. AuditLogs has `OperationName`, `Category`, `LoggedByService`, `Result`, `InitiatedBy`, `TargetResources`.

Core operators:
- `where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)` filters time.
- `summarize count() by AppDisplayName` aggregates.
- `summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)` buckets time; `render timechart` charts it.
- `project` picks columns; `extend` adds computed columns; `top 10 by` ranks; `distinct` dedupes.

Example: failed sign-ins per user today:
`SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) | where ResultType != "0" | summarize Failures = count() by UserPrincipalName | top 10 by Failures`.
Save a query as an **Azure Monitor alert rule** (custom log search) for notifications, as with break-glass monitoring.

terms.d: Kusto Query Language used in Log Analytics.
KQL operator that aggregates rows, e.g. count() by column.
KQL function returning a time relative to now.

lessons.trap: Interactive and non-interactive user sign-ins are different tables; a query on SigninLogs alone misses token-based sign-ins.
lessons.example: A query counts sign-ins with ConditionalAccessStatus == "failure" by app to find which policy is blocking a rollout.

lessons.title: Workbooks and reporting
lessons.short: **Workbooks** are Azure Monitor dashboards over Entra logs in Log Analytics.
