questions.explain: Microsoft recommends including any device and excluding supported platforms, then blocking, because unsupported platforms like ChromeOS can't be selected directly. Including supported platforms with Block would block the wrong devices.
options: Include Any device and require a compliant device
Include Any device, exclude Windows, macOS, iOS and Android, and grant Block access
Include Windows, macOS, iOS and Android and grant Block access
Include ChromeOS only and grant Block access

questions.stem: Which events are critical events that CAE-capable services evaluate in near real time? Select THREE.
questions.explain: Critical events include account disabled or deleted, password change or reset, MFA enabled, admin token revocation and high user risk. Profile photo changes aren't events, and group membership changes can take much longer to apply.
options: An administrator revokes the user's refresh tokens
High user risk is detected by ID Protection
The user changes their profile photo
The user joins a new Microsoft 365 group
The user account is disabled

questions.stem: A Conditional Access policy blocks Exchange Online access outside a country/region named location. With CAE enabled, a user moves to a blocked country mid-session. What happens?
questions.explain: CAE instant location enforcement supports IP-range named locations only; country/region locations fall back to normal token lifetime. Instant rejection would occur for an IP-based location.
options: The session is terminated after 15 minutes
The user is prompted for MFA immediately
Access continues until the token expires because CAE enforces only IP-based named locations
Exchange Online rejects the token instantly

questions.stem: For each statement about continuous access evaluation, select Yes if true.
questions.explain: CAE clients get long-lived tokens up to 28 hours. Guest users aren't supported. The Disable option works only with All resources and no conditions.

statements.s: CAE-capable clients can receive tokens valid for up to 28 hours.
CAE is enforced instantly for B2B guest users.
CAE can be disabled with the Customize continuous access evaluation session control in a policy targeting All resources.

questions.case: Woodgrove enabled a Conditional Access policy that allows SharePoint only from its trusted HQ named location. Remote staff connect through a split-tunnel VPN; only some traffic goes through the HQ egress IPs.
questions.stem: After enabling an IP-based location policy with CAE, remote users on a split-tunnel VPN are intermittently blocked from SharePoint with insufficient_claims errors. What is the most likely fix?
questions.explain: Split tunnelling makes Entra ID and SharePoint see different IPs, so CAE's instant IP enforcement fails. Microsoft advises listing all dedicated egress IPs, including IPv6. Converting to country/region would remove the IP control.
options: Enable persistent browser sessions
Disable sign-in frequency in the policy
Convert the named location to a country/region location
Add all of the VPN's IPv4 and IPv6 egress addresses to the trusted named location

questions.stem: A SharePoint site containing merger documents must require a compliant device, but the rest of SharePoint must not. What should you create first?
questions.explain: Authentication context lets you apply a Conditional Access policy to a specific site through a sensitivity label or site setting. Targeting Office 365 would affect all of SharePoint; SharePoint sites aren't separate enterprise apps.
options: An authentication context, then a Conditional Access policy targeting it
A named location for the site
A Conditional Access policy targeting the Office 365 app group
A separate enterprise application for the site

questions.stem: For each statement about authentication context, select Yes if true.
questions.explain: IDs range c1-c99. Publish to apps controls whether apps can use the context. Before deletion, remove it from policies and unpublish it.

statements.s: You can create up to 99 authentication contexts with IDs c1 to c99.
Clearing Publish to apps makes the context unavailable for assignment by downstream apps.
A context can be deleted while Conditional Access policies still reference it.

questions.stem: Complete the Microsoft Graph Conditional Access policy JSON so it applies to authentication context c1.
questions.explain: Authentication contexts are targeted with includeAuthenticationContextClassReferences under applications. includeApplications takes app IDs, includeUserActions takes user actions, and authenticationStrength belongs to grantControls.
options: "includeApplications": ["c1"]
"includeAuthenticationContextClassReferences": ["c1"]
"authenticationStrength": { "id": "c1" }
"includeUserActions": ["c1"]

questions.stem: You want admins to perform a FIDO2 step-up immediately before they can delete Conditional Access policies, regardless of which role they hold. What should you configure?
questions.explain: Protected actions require a Conditional Access policy (via authentication context) when the permission is used, independent of role. PIM settings apply only at activation; Admin Portals applies at sign-in; removing the permission changes authorisation, not authentication.
options: A PIM activation setting requiring MFA
A custom role without the delete permission
A protected action linked to an authentication context
A Conditional Access policy targeting Microsoft Admin Portals

questions.stem: Put the steps to configure a protected action in order.
questions.explain: Microsoft warns skipping order can cause repeated prompts: create the context, build the policy, map it to protected permissions, then test.
options: Create an authentication context
Create a Conditional Access policy that targets the authentication context
Assign the authentication context to the selected permissions in Protected actions
Sign in as an admin and perform the action to test the step-up prompt

questions.stem: Which permissions can be configured as protected actions? Select TWO.
questions.explain: Protected actions cover Conditional Access policy management, cross-tenant access settings, hard deletes, named locations and authentication context updates. Reading logs, creating users and password resets aren't in the protectable set.
options: Resetting a non-admin user's password
Hard deletion of directory objects
Updating Conditional Access policies
Creating a new user account
Reading the sign-in logs

questions.stem: In which state is a Conditional Access policy created from a template?
questions.explain: Template policies are created in report-only so you can review the impact before turning them on.
options: Disabled until approved by a Global Administrator
Off
On
Report-only

questions.stem: You create the Require multifactor authentication for all users policy from a template. Which accounts are excluded automatically?
questions.explain: Templates exclude only the creating user; you must edit the policy to exclude break-glass accounts. Admins and guests are not excluded.
options: Only the administrator who created the policy
All emergency access accounts
All guest users
All accounts with directory roles

questions.stem: Microsoft recommends a risk-based Conditional Access policy for user risk. Which configuration matches the recommendation?
questions.explain: The recommended user risk policy targets High risk, requires risk remediation (or MFA plus secure password change) and enforces sign-in frequency Every time. Blocking at Low creates excessive lockouts; compliance and terms of use don't remediate risk.
options: User risk High; grant Require terms of use; persistent browser session
User risk High; grant Require risk remediation; sign-in frequency Every time
User risk Low and above; grant Block access
User risk Medium and High; grant Require device to be marked as compliant

questions.stem: For each statement about user risk remediation, select Yes if true.
questions.explain: Users must be MFA-registered before remediation or they're blocked. Hybrid users need password writeback. Only a secure password change inside the remediation flow satisfies the control.

statements.s: A user who isn't registered for MFA can self-remediate high user risk by changing their password.
For synced hybrid users, password writeback is required for the secure password change to remediate risk.
A password change made outside the risk remediation flow satisfies the Require password change control.

questions.stem: Your tenant still uses the legacy user risk policy in the ID Protection dashboard. What does Microsoft advise before its retirement on 1 October 2026?
questions.explain: Microsoft recommends recreating risk policies in Conditional Access, validating in report-only, enforcing, then setting the legacy policy to Disabled. There's no automatic migration, and campaigns or PIM don't evaluate risk.
options: Move the policy to Privileged Identity Management
Convert the legacy policy into a registration campaign
Create equivalent Conditional Access risk policies in report-only, enable them, then disable the legacy policy
Leave the legacy policy enabled; it migrates automatically

questions.case: Litware synchronises identities with password hash sync. Most users reset passwords from their domain-joined PCs with Ctrl+Alt+Delete rather than through SSPR.
questions.stem: Hybrid users use password hash sync. They often reset passwords on-premises with Ctrl+Alt+Delete after being flagged as risky, but their user risk stays high. What should you enable?
questions.explain: This ID Protection setting lets an on-premises password change (synced via PHS) remediate user risk. Seamless SSO, writeback unlock and smart lockout don't affect risk state.
options: Seamless single sign-on
Self-service password reset writeback unlock
Smart lockout customisation
Allow on-premises password change to reset user risk

questions.stem: You need a Conditional Access policy that challenges risky sign-ins according to Microsoft's recommendation. Which sign-in risk levels should you include?
questions.explain: Microsoft recommends requiring MFA (authentication strength) for Medium and High sign-in risk. High only misses many attacks; including Low creates prompt fatigue.
options: Medium and High
Low, Medium and High
High only
No risk and above

questions.stem: Which detections are sign-in risk detections (not user risk detections)? Select TWO.
questions.explain: Atypical travel and anonymous IP address are sign-in risk detections. Leaked credentials, PRT access attempts and user-reported suspicious activity are user risk detections.
options: Leaked credentials
Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token
User reported suspicious activity
Anonymous IP address
Atypical travel

questions.stem: For each statement about sign-in risk, select Yes if true.
questions.explain: Passing MFA remediates sign-in risk. Non-P2 tenants see premium detections as Additional risk detected. Microsoft advises separate policies for user and sign-in risk.

statements.s: A user who completes MFA on a risky sign-in self-remediates that sign-in's risk.
Without Entra ID P2, premium detections appear as Additional risk detected.
Microsoft recommends combining user risk and sign-in risk conditions in one policy.

questions.stem: Complete the Conditional Access policy JSON condition so the policy applies to medium and high sign-in risk.
questions.explain: Sign-in risk is set with signInRiskLevels. userRiskLevels is for user risk, servicePrincipalRiskLevels for workload identities, and riskLevels isn't a valid property.
options: "servicePrincipalRiskLevels": ["medium", "high"]
"signInRiskLevels": ["medium", "high"]
"userRiskLevels": ["medium", "high"]
"riskLevels": { "signIn": "medium" }

questions.stem: You want to nudge users who currently use SMS for MFA to set up Microsoft Authenticator during sign-in, allowing them to postpone a few times. What should you configure?
questions.explain: Registration campaigns nudge users to a specific method (Authenticator or passkey) with snoozes. The ID Protection policy requires any MFA registration, the CA user action secures registration, and system-preferred MFA picks among registered methods.
options: The ID Protection MFA registration policy
A Conditional Access policy for Register security information
A registration campaign targeting Microsoft Authenticator
System-preferred multifactor authentication

questions.stem: For each statement about registration campaigns, select Yes if true.
questions.explain: Snooze days range 0-14. A campaign targets one method at a time. Limited snoozes enforce registration after three snoozes.

statements.s: Days allowed to snooze can be set from 0 to 14.
A campaign can target Microsoft Authenticator and passkeys at the same time.
With Limited number of snoozes on, users must register after snoozing three times.

questions.case: Tailwind Traders has 3,000 users, 400 of whom haven't registered MFA. Several accounts were compromised through password spray and an attacker-controlled Authenticator was registered on them.
questions.stem: Attackers with stolen passwords are registering their own Authenticator apps on accounts that have no MFA method yet. Which control best prevents this?
questions.explain: Protecting the Register security information action stops registration from untrusted contexts. A campaign or the MFA registration policy would actually push the attacker to register; Report suspicious activity relies on an existing method.
options: A registration campaign with 0 snooze days
The ID Protection MFA registration policy
Report suspicious activity
A Conditional Access policy targeting the Register security information user action that requires a trusted location or compliant device

questions.stem: ID Protection flags a user as high risk, but you confirm the activity was the user on a business trip. You want to clear the risk without forcing a password change. Which action should you take?
questions.explain: Dismiss user risk clears the risk state without changing the password, appropriate for false positives. Confirm compromised escalates risk; Reset password and Block are for real compromises.
options: Dismiss user risk
Confirm user compromised
Reset password
Block user

questions.stem: Complete the Microsoft Graph PowerShell command to list all users currently at high risk.
questions.explain: Get-MgRiskyUser returns risky user objects with RiskLevel and RiskState. Get-MgRiskDetection returns individual detections, Get-MgUser has no risk data, and Get-MgRiskyServicePrincipal is for workload identities.
options: Get-MgRiskyServicePrincipal
Get-MgRiskyUser
Get-MgUser
Get-MgRiskDetection

questions.case: An analyst confirms that an attacker accessed Megan's account from overseas and registered an extra MFA method. No risk policy fired because the tenant's risk policies were in report-only.
questions.stem: An investigation confirms a user's account was compromised and no policy remediated it. Put Microsoft's recommended response in order.
questions.explain: Mark the user compromised to feed the model, force a new password (or block), revoke refresh tokens so stolen sessions end, then disable compromised devices.
options: Confirm the user compromised in ID Protection
Require a password change (block the user if the attacker may control MFA)
Revoke the user's refresh tokens
Disable devices the attacker may have used

questions.stem: Which ID Protection report shows every individual detection, including whether it was real-time or offline?
questions.explain: The Risk detections report lists each detection with its type and timing. Risky users summarises per user, Risky sign-ins lists sign-ins, and Authentication methods activity covers registration and usage.
options: Risky sign-ins
Risky users
Risk detections
Authentication methods activity

questions.stem: You want to block a single-tenant service principal from signing in when ID Protection rates it high risk. What do you need?
questions.explain: Risk-based Conditional Access for service principals needs Workload Identities Premium and a policy scoped to workload identities using service principal risk. User and sign-in risk policies don't apply to service principals.
options: Entra ID P2 and a user risk policy that includes the app
Workload Identities Premium and an ID Protection user risk policy
Entra ID P1 and a sign-in risk policy for All users
Workload Identities Premium and a Conditional Access policy assigned to workload identities with service principal risk

questions.stem: For each statement about risky workload identities, select Yes if true.
questions.explain: Managed identities aren't in scope. Workload identity CA applies only to single-tenant service principals registered in your tenant. Leaked credentials flags exposed app credentials.

statements.s: Managed identities are currently in scope for workload identity risk detections.
Conditional Access for workload identities can target multitenant apps from other publishers.
Leaked credentials detects app secrets or certificates found in public code repositories.

questions.case: A secret for the Contoso-Payroll-Sync app registration was committed to a public GitHub repository. ID Protection raised a Leaked credentials detection for the service principal.
questions.stem: A service principal's client secret was found in a public repository. Put Microsoft's remediation steps in order.
questions.explain: Inventory first so nothing is missed, add the replacement credential before removing the old one to avoid outage, remove the leaked credential, then rotate downstream secrets.
options: Inventory the credentials on the service principal and application objects
Add a new credential, preferably an X.509 certificate
Remove the compromised credentials
Rotate any Azure Key Vault secrets the service principal can access

questions.stem: Users on Microsoft Entra registered (not joined) Windows 11 devices install the Global Secure Access client. Which traffic will the client acquire?
questions.explain: On Entra registered devices the Windows client supports only Private Access traffic. Joined or hybrid joined devices are needed for the full set of profiles.
options: Private Access traffic only
All traffic forwarding profiles
Microsoft traffic only
Internet Access traffic only

questions.stem: Microsoft recommends configuring endpoints before using Microsoft Entra Internet Access through the Global Secure Access client. Which browser or network features should you disable? Select TWO.
questions.explain: Internet Access doesn't support QUIC or DNS over HTTPS, so Microsoft recommends disabling both. TLS 1.2, IPv4 and HTTP/1.1 are needed; IPv4 should be preferred over IPv6.
options: QUIC (UDP 443)
IPv4
DNS over HTTPS
TLS 1.2
HTTP/1.1

questions.stem: A branch office has printers and IoT devices that can't run the Global Secure Access client. You need their Microsoft 365 and internet traffic secured by Global Secure Access. What should you configure?
questions.explain: Remote networks connect a site's CPE to Global Secure Access over IPsec/BGP, without clients, for Microsoft and Internet Access profiles. Connectors and Quick Access are for Private Access inbound to apps; named locations don't forward traffic.
options: A private network connector in the branch
A remote network with an IPsec tunnel from the branch router
An IP-based named location for the branch
Quick Access with the branch subnet

questions.stem: On Android devices, how is the Global Secure Access client delivered?
questions.explain: The Android Global Secure Access client is built into the Microsoft Defender app and deployed with an Intune app configuration policy. Authenticator and Company Portal don't provide it.
options: Built into Microsoft Authenticator
Through the Company Portal VPN profile
As part of the Microsoft Defender app, configured through Intune
As a standalone Global Secure Access app from Google Play

questions.stem: You want to replace a legacy VPN quickly by giving users access to the whole 10.10.0.0/16 network through Microsoft Entra Private Access, then later apply per-application policies. What should you configure first?
questions.explain: Quick Access is the fast VPN replacement holding broad segments; Microsoft calls it a transition state before per-app access. Per-app first is slower, and the Microsoft profile or remote networks don't publish private apps.
options: The Microsoft traffic profile
A remote network for the datacenter
Per-app Global Secure Access enterprise applications for every server
Quick Access with an IP range application segment

questions.stem: For each statement about Microsoft Entra Private Access, select Yes if true.
questions.explain: Connectors make outbound-only connections. Nested groups aren't supported for assignment. Enterprise app segments win over overlapping Quick Access segments.

statements.s: Private network connectors require inbound firewall ports opened from the internet.
Users who get access only through a nested group are granted access to a Private Access app.
A per-app enterprise application segment takes priority over an overlapping Quick Access segment.

questions.stem: Put the high-level steps to publish an app with Microsoft Entra Private Access in order.
questions.explain: Microsoft's order: connectors, app and segments, assignments, Conditional Access, then turn on the Private Access forwarding profile so the client starts tunnelling.
options: Create a connector group with at least one active private network connector
Create the Global Secure Access application and add application segments
Assign users and groups to the application
Create Conditional Access policies for the application
Enable the Private Access traffic forwarding profile

questions.case: Tailwind's intranet apps are reached by short names such as http://benefits. Private Access already has an IP range segment covering 10.8.0.0/16, which contains the app servers.
questions.stem: Users must reach an internal app at http://benefits (a short name) through Private Access, without defining every host as an FQDN segment. The app's IP is inside a configured IP range segment. What should you configure?
questions.explain: Private DNS adds DNS suffixes so the client resolves and routes short names. NetBIOS names aren't supported as segments, a bare * isn't valid, and named locations don't route traffic.
options: Private DNS with the internal DNS suffix
A NetBIOS name application segment
A named location for the IP range
A wildcard FQDN segment of *

questions.stem: You must block the Gambling web category for all users and all remote network traffic without creating a Conditional Access policy. Where should you link the web content filtering policy?
questions.explain: The baseline profile applies tenant-wide to all Internet Access traffic, including remote networks, with no CA policy. Other security profiles reach users through Conditional Access. The Microsoft profile covers Microsoft 365 only.
options: The Microsoft traffic profile
The baseline profile
A TLS inspection policy
A security profile linked to a Conditional Access policy

questions.stem: Put the steps to block a web category for one group using Microsoft Entra Internet Access in order.
questions.explain: Traffic must be forwarded first; then build the policy, group it in a security profile, and deliver the profile to the group through Conditional Access targeting All internet resources with Global Secure Access.
options: Enable the Internet Access traffic forwarding profile
Create a web content filtering policy with a block rule for the category
Add the filtering policy to a security profile
Create a Conditional Access policy for the group with the Use Global Secure Access security profile session control

questions.stem: For each statement about Microsoft Entra Internet Access, select Yes if true.
questions.explain: Block takes precedence in conflicts. FQDN filtering uses SNI and works without TLS inspection. TLS inspection requires devices to trust the inspecting CA's root certificate.

statements.s: When an allow rule and a block rule conflict, block wins.
FQDN-based web filtering of HTTPS sites requires TLS inspection.
Devices must trust the root certificate used for TLS inspection.

questions.stem: You want to block access to Exchange Online unless the traffic arrives through your tenant's Global Secure Access, without maintaining IP lists. What should you configure?
questions.explain: The compliant network check is tenant-specific and needs no IP lists. Edge IPs are shared and change; Bypass would stop forwarding; tenant restrictions control which tenants users sign in to, not network origin.
options: Set the Exchange Online policy group to Bypass
Enable universal tenant restrictions
Enable Conditional Access signaling and block all locations except All Compliant Network locations
Create an IP-based named location with the Global Secure Access edge IPs

questions.stem: For each statement about the Microsoft traffic profile, select Yes if true.
questions.explain: Policy groups are Exchange Online, SharePoint/OneDrive, Teams and M365 Common/Office Online. Bypassed Microsoft traffic goes direct and isn't acquired by Internet Access. The profile fails open unless you enforce compliant network.

statements.s: Microsoft Teams is one of the policy groups in the Microsoft traffic profile.
If an FQDN in the Microsoft traffic profile is set to Bypass, the Internet Access profile acquires it instead.
If the client can't connect to the service, Microsoft traffic fails open and goes direct.

questions.case: Contoso is worried about data exfiltration to personal or attacker-controlled Microsoft 365 tenants. All corporate laptops run the Global Secure Access client. Partner Fabrikam must remain accessible.
questions.stem: Employees must be prevented from signing in to Microsoft 365 tenants other than your own and approved partners from any device running the Global Secure Access client. What should you configure?
questions.explain: Universal tenant restrictions enforce TRv2 through Global Secure Access when the Microsoft profile is on. Cross-tenant sync provisions users; compliant network checks origin, not target tenant; external collaboration settings govern guest invitations.
options: External collaboration settings with a domain allow list
Cross-tenant synchronization
The compliant network check
Tenant restrictions v2 in cross-tenant access settings plus universal tenant restrictions with the Microsoft traffic profile

questions.stem: Which identity is deleted automatically when the Azure virtual machine it belongs to is deleted?
options: A user-assigned managed identity attached to the VM
The VM's system-assigned managed identity
A service principal created from an app registration
A group managed service account used by the VM
questions.explain: A system-assigned managed identity shares the lifecycle of its resource and is deleted with it. A user-assigned identity is a separate resource that must be deleted explicitly. App registrations and gMSAs are unrelated to the VM's lifecycle.

questions.stem: Twenty Azure Functions apps need identical read access to one key vault. The function apps are torn down and recreated weekly. You want the fewest role assignments and no credentials to manage. Which identity should you use?
options: A system-assigned managed identity on each function app
An app registration with a client secret stored in app settings
One user-assigned managed identity attached to all function apps
A user account excluded from MFA used by all function apps
questions.explain: A user-assigned managed identity survives the function apps being recreated, and one role assignment covers all of them. System-assigned identities would need new role assignments after every rebuild. A client secret or a user account adds credentials to manage and is less secure.

questions.stem: A Windows service runs on four on-premises servers in an Active Directory domain. It needs one domain identity whose password is rotated automatically and never known to administrators. What should you use?
options: A group managed service account (gMSA)
A standalone managed service account (sMSA)
A system-assigned managed identity
A service principal with a certificate
questions.explain: A gMSA is an AD account that several hosts can share, with automatic password management. An sMSA is limited to a single computer. Managed identities and service principals are Entra ID identities and don't provide a domain identity for an on-premises Windows service.

questions.case: Litware runs a reporting job on a Linux server in a third-party colocation datacenter. The server isn't Azure Arc-enabled and has no Azure footprint. The job must upload files to an Azure Storage account every hour. Security policy forbids user accounts for automation and prefers credentials that are hard to exfiltrate.
questions.stem: Which identity should the job use?
options: A system-assigned managed identity enabled on the server
A user-assigned managed identity assigned to the server
A dedicated cloud user account excluded from Conditional Access
An app registration whose service principal authenticates with a certificate
questions.explain: Managed identities can be attached only to Azure resources (or Arc-enabled servers), so they aren't available here. A service principal with a certificate works from anywhere and is stronger than a secret. A user account breaks the policy.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about user-assigned managed identities are true? Select TWO.
options: They can be assigned to multiple Azure resources at the same time.
They are deleted automatically when the last resource using them is deleted.
They require you to rotate a client secret periodically.
They are created as standalone Azure resources in a resource group.
questions.explain: User-assigned identities are their own Azure resources and can be shared across many resources. They have an independent lifecycle, so they persist until you delete them. Like all managed identities, their credentials are handled by Azure, so there's no secret to rotate.

questions.stem: For each statement, select Yes if true.

statements.s: A managed identity is represented in Microsoft Entra ID as a special type of service principal.
A single system-assigned managed identity can be shared by two virtual machines.
The Managed Identity Contributor role allows a user to create user-assigned managed identities.

questions.explain: Every managed identity is backed by a service principal of type ManagedIdentity. A system-assigned identity belongs to exactly one resource. Managed Identity Contributor can create, update and delete user-assigned identities, while Managed Identity Operator can only read and assign them.

questions.stem: Complete the Azure CLI command to create a user-assigned managed identity named id-orders.
options: create
assign
add
new
questions.explain: `az identity create` creates a user-assigned managed identity resource. `assign` is used with `az vm identity` or `az webapp identity` to attach identities to compute. `add` and `new` aren't valid subcommands of `az identity`.

questions.stem: You need to enable the system-assigned managed identity on an existing VM named vm1. Complete the command.
options: create
enable
assign
set
questions.explain: `az vm identity assign` without `--identities` enables the system-assigned identity. Adding `--identities <resource ID>` attaches a user-assigned identity instead. `create`, `enable` and `set` aren't subcommands of `az vm identity`.

questions.stem: A platform engineer must attach an existing user-assigned managed identity to VMs. The engineer must not be able to create or delete managed identities. Which role should you grant on the identity, following least privilege?
options: Managed Identity Contributor
User Access Administrator
Reader
Managed Identity Operator
questions.explain: Managed Identity Operator can read and assign user-assigned identities but can't create or delete them. Managed Identity Contributor can create and delete, which exceeds the requirement. Reader can't assign. User Access Administrator manages role assignments and doesn't attach identities.

questions.stem: An app on an Azure VM must read blobs by using the VM's system-assigned managed identity. Put the steps in order.
options: Enable the system-assigned managed identity on the VM
Assign the Storage Blob Data Reader role to the VM's identity on the storage account
Have the app request a token from IMDS for https://storage.azure.com/
Call the Blob service REST API with the token as a bearer token
questions.explain: The identity must exist before it can receive a role. The role assignment authorizes it on the data plane. The app then gets a token for the storage resource from the Instance Metadata Service and presents that token to Azure Storage.

questions.stem: Code on an Azure VM must get a managed identity token for Azure Key Vault. Complete the request.
options: Authorization:Bearer
Content-Type:application/json
X-IDENTITY-HEADER:true
Metadata:true
questions.explain: IMDS requires the header `Metadata: true` (lowercase true) to block server-side request forgery. There's no bearer token yet, because that's what you're requesting. X-IDENTITY-HEADER is used by the App Service endpoint, not by IMDS on a VM.

questions.case: VM-Batch01 has no system-assigned identity and has two user-assigned managed identities: id-reader and id-writer. Only id-writer has the Storage Blob Data Contributor role. A script's token request to IMDS fails because it doesn't say which identity to use.
questions.stem: Complete the request so that the token is issued for id-writer.
options: tenant_id
client_id
principal_name
identity_id
questions.explain: When a VM has several user-assigned identities, the request must name one with `client_id`, `object_id` or `msi_res_id`. Here the value is a client ID, so `client_id` is correct. `tenant_id`, `principal_name` and `identity_id` aren't IMDS identity selector parameters.

questions.stem: For each statement, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Code on an Azure VM can obtain a token for its managed identity without storing any secret or certificate.
Assigning the Contributor role on a storage account is enough for a managed identity to read blob data with Microsoft Entra authorization.
A managed identity can be used directly by an on-premises server that isn't Azure Arc-enabled.

questions.explain: Managed identity tokens come from IMDS with no stored credential. Contributor is a control-plane role, and blob data access needs a data role such as Storage Blob Data Reader. Managed identities are available only on Azure resources or Azure Arc-enabled servers.

questions.stem: Which enterprise application property, when set to No, prevents all users from signing in to the app, even if they are assigned, and stops token issuance for it?
options: Visible to users?
Assignment required?
Enabled for users to sign in?
Owners
questions.explain: 'Enabled for users to sign in?' maps to accountEnabled. Setting it to No disables the service principal, so nobody can sign in or get tokens. 'Assignment required?' only limits access to assigned principals. 'Visible to users?' only hides the My Apps tile.

questions.stem: A SAML enterprise app is assigned to the Legal group. Users outside Legal can still sign in to it. You need only assigned users to get tokens. What should you do?
options: Set 'Assignment required?' to Yes
Set 'Visible to users?' to No
Remove the app from all My Apps collections
Set 'Enabled for users to sign in?' to No
questions.explain: When 'Assignment required?' is No, any user in the tenant can sign in. Setting it to Yes restricts tokens to assigned principals. Hiding the app or removing it from collections changes only visibility. Disabling sign-in would block the Legal users too.

questions.stem: For each statement about enterprise app properties, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Setting 'Visible to users?' to No prevents assigned users from signing in to the app.
The Notes property has no effect on sign-in behavior.
When 'Assignment required?' is No for an OIDC app, guest users in the tenant can also sign in to it.

questions.explain: Visibility only controls the My Apps and Microsoft 365 launcher tile, so users can still sign in by URL. Notes is free text for administrators. With assignment not required, any user in the tenant can sign in, including invited external (guest) users.

questions.stem: Users are creating unmanaged app registrations. You must stop regular users from registering applications but still let the 12-person development team create them, using least privilege. What should you do?
options: Set 'Users can register applications' to No and assign the Cloud Application Administrator role to the developers
Set 'Users can register applications' to No and assign the Application Developer role to the developers
Disable user consent and enable the admin consent workflow
Set 'Users can register applications' to No and make the developers owners of existing apps
questions.explain: Application Developer can create registrations regardless of the tenant setting and is the least-privileged fit. Cloud Application Administrator can manage every app in the tenant, which is too much. Consent settings don't control registration. Owning existing apps doesn't let users create new ones.

questions.stem: Which Microsoft Entra built-in role can manage all aspects of app registrations and enterprise apps EXCEPT Application Proxy?
options: Application Administrator
Application Developer
Cloud Application Administrator
Hybrid Identity Administrator
questions.explain: Cloud Application Administrator matches Application Administrator except for Application Proxy. Application Administrator includes App Proxy. Application Developer can only create registrations and manage the ones it owns. Hybrid Identity Administrator manages sync and federation, not enterprise apps.

questions.stem: An administrator must publish on-premises web apps through Microsoft Entra application proxy and manage their connector groups. Which role should you assign, following least privilege?
options: Global Administrator
Application Administrator
Cloud Application Administrator
Security Administrator
questions.explain: Application Administrator includes Application Proxy settings and is the least-privileged built-in role for this task. Cloud Application Administrator specifically excludes App Proxy. Global Administrator works but is excessive. Security Administrator manages security features, not app publishing.

questions.stem: A team lead must configure SSO and manage user assignments for the HR enterprise app only. They must not be able to manage other apps. Which TWO actions meet the requirement? Select TWO.
options: Add the team lead as an owner of the HR enterprise app
Assign the Cloud Application Administrator role at tenant scope
Assign the Application Developer role at tenant scope
Assign the Cloud Application Administrator role scoped to the HR app only
Add the team lead to the Users and groups assignment of the HR app
questions.explain: Owners can manage the specific app they own, and app-scoped role assignments limit the role to that one app. A tenant-wide Cloud Application Administrator assignment covers every app. Application Developer can't manage SSO for an existing app it doesn't own. Being assigned as a user only grants sign-in.

questions.stem: For each statement, select Yes if true.

statements.s: A user with the Application Developer role can create app registrations even when 'Users can register applications' is set to No.
A user with the Cloud Application Administrator role can configure Application Proxy settings for an app.
An owner of an enterprise application can manage that application without holding an Entra admin role.

questions.explain: Application Developer ignores the 'Users can register applications' setting. Cloud Application Administrator excludes Application Proxy, which requires Application Administrator. Object-level owners can manage the app they own.

questions.stem: Which component must you install on-premises to publish an internal web app through Microsoft Entra application proxy?
options: Microsoft Entra Connect Health agent
Microsoft Entra private network connector
Microsoft Entra provisioning agent
Microsoft Entra Connect Sync
questions.explain: Application proxy relays traffic through the Microsoft Entra private network connector, the same connector used by Global Secure Access Private Access. The provisioning agent is used for Cloud Sync and on-premises provisioning. Connect Sync and the Connect Health agent handle directory sync and monitoring.

questions.stem: Your network team asks what firewall changes the application proxy connector server needs. What should you tell them?
options: Allow inbound TCP 443 from the internet to the connector server
Place the connector server in a perimeter network and allow inbound TCP 80
Allow outbound TCP 443 (and 80 for CRL checks) from the connector server; no inbound ports are needed
Create a site-to-site VPN between the connector server and Azure
questions.explain: The connector makes outbound connections only: 443 to the service and 80 for certificate revocation lists. No inbound ports, perimeter network or VPN are needed. That's a main benefit of application proxy.

questions.stem: You are publishing an on-premises intranet site with Microsoft Entra application proxy. Put the steps in order.
options: Install and register the private network connector on a Windows server that can reach the site
In Enterprise apps, select Add an on-premises application and enter the internal and external URLs
Set Pre Authentication to Microsoft Entra ID and select the connector group
Assign users or groups to the new enterprise app
Browse to the external URL as an assigned user to test access
questions.explain: A registered connector must exist before the app can use a connector group. You create the on-premises app with its URLs, set pre-authentication and the connector group, assign users who are allowed to sign in, and then test through the external URL.

questions.case: Tailspin publishes a claims-processing site through application proxy with Pre Authentication set to Passthrough. Auditors require MFA through Conditional Access for every external session. They also require real-time session monitoring through Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps.
questions.stem: What should you change first?
options: Set Pre Authentication to Microsoft Entra ID
Configure Kerberos constrained delegation on the connector
Move the app to a new connector group
Enable header-based single sign-on
questions.explain: With Passthrough, Entra ID doesn't authenticate users, so Conditional Access and Defender for Cloud Apps can't apply. Entra ID pre-authentication is required for both. KCD and header-based SSO handle back-end sign-in, and connector groups handle routing.

questions.stem: An on-premises app published through application proxy uses Integrated Windows Authentication. Users are prompted again after Entra sign-in. What should you configure to provide SSO?
options: Password-based single sign-on
SAML-based single sign-on
Header-based single sign-on
Kerberos constrained delegation for the connector's computer account
questions.explain: For IWA apps, the connector gets Kerberos tickets for users through Kerberos constrained delegation (KCD), which removes the second prompt. Password-based SSO is for form logins, SAML for federation-capable apps, and header-based SSO for apps that read identity from HTTP headers.

questions.stem: You are configuring SAML SSO for a gallery app. Which TWO values are required in the Basic SAML Configuration section? Select TWO.
options: Identifier (Entity ID)
Redirect URI for a single-page application
Client secret
Reply URL (Assertion Consumer Service URL)
Application ID URI for an exposed API
questions.explain: SAML requires the service provider's Identifier (Entity ID) and the Reply URL (ACS) where Entra ID posts the assertion. Redirect URIs, client secrets and Application ID URIs belong to OAuth and OIDC app registrations, not SAML configuration.

questions.case: Contoso enabled the admin consent workflow and made Ben, a Cloud Application Administrator, a reviewer. A user requests consent for a reporting tool that asks for the Microsoft Graph application permission Reports.Read.All. Ben can see the request but can't approve it.
questions.stem: What is the most likely reason?
options: Admin consent requests can be approved only by the user who submitted them
The request expired the moment Ben opened it
The app must be removed from the My Apps collection before approval
Granting Microsoft Graph application permissions needs a higher-privileged role than Cloud Application Administrator
questions.explain: Being a reviewer doesn't grant consent rights. Consent for Microsoft Graph application permissions (app roles) needs a higher-privileged role, such as Global Administrator. Requesters can't approve their own requests, opening a request doesn't expire it, and collections are irrelevant.

questions.stem: Sales staff want their CRM, quoting and e-signature apps grouped on one tab in the My Apps portal. What should you configure?
options: An administrative unit containing the three apps
A collection in Enterprise apps > App launchers, assigned to the Sales group
An access package catalog containing the three apps
Company branding for the Sales group
questions.explain: Collections, created under App launchers, add named tabs to My Apps and are assigned to users or groups. Administrative units scope admin rights. Access package catalogs govern access requests. Company branding changes the sign-in page.

questions.stem: Using Microsoft Graph PowerShell, you must assign a user to the Approver app role of an enterprise app. Complete the command.
options: New-MgServicePrincipalOwnerByRef
New-MgOauth2PermissionGrant
New-MgUserAppRoleAssignment
New-MgGroupMember
questions.explain: New-MgUserAppRoleAssignment creates an app role assignment for a user. The resource is the app's service principal and the AppRoleId is the role. The owner cmdlet adds owners, an OAuth2 permission grant records delegated consent, and New-MgGroupMember changes group membership.

questions.stem: A gallery SaaS app supports SCIM 2.0. Accounts must be created when users are assigned and deactivated when they're unassigned or disabled. What should you configure?
options: Just-in-time provisioning through the app's SAML configuration
Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync for the app
Automatic provisioning on the app's Provisioning tab with the tenant URL and secret token
A dynamic group assigned to the app with Visible to users set to Yes
questions.explain: Automatic provisioning uses SCIM to create, update and deactivate accounts for in-scope users. SAML JIT provisioning creates accounts at first sign-in but never deprovisions them. Cloud Sync syncs AD to Entra ID, not to SaaS apps. A dynamic group alone doesn't create accounts in the app.

questions.stem: For each statement about assigning access to enterprise apps, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Assigning a group to an enterprise app requires Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2.
When you assign a group to an app, members of groups nested inside it also get access.
Provisioning can be scoped to sync only assigned users and groups.

questions.explain: Group-based app assignment is a P1 feature. Only direct members of an assigned group get access, because nested groups aren't expanded. Provisioning settings offer 'Sync only assigned users and groups', which is the recommended scope.

questions.case: Developers defined two app roles, Reader and Approver, in the Expenses app registration. The app grants approval rights only when the token's roles claim contains Approver. The Finance-Managers security group must get approval rights.
questions.stem: What should you do?
options: Add Finance-Managers as an owner of the Expenses app registration
Add a groups optional claim to the Expenses app's token configuration
Create a dynamic group named Approver and add the managers to it
In Enterprise apps > Expenses > Users and groups, assign Finance-Managers with the Approver role
questions.explain: Assigning the group to the enterprise app with the Approver role makes Entra ID put Approver in members' roles claim. Owners can manage the app but don't get roles. A groups claim emits group IDs, not app roles. Naming a group 'Approver' doesn't map it to the role.

questions.stem: Users should consent only to apps from verified publishers, and only for permissions you've classified as low impact. Everything else should go to an admin. Which user consent setting should you choose?
options: Do not allow user consent
Allow user consent for apps
Allow user consent for apps from verified publishers, for selected permissions
Users can request admin consent to apps they are unable to consent to
questions.explain: This option applies the built-in low-impact policy: users consent only to apps from verified publishers (or registered in your tenant) and only for classified low-impact permissions. 'Do not allow' blocks all user consent, 'Allow user consent for apps' is too broad, and the last option is an admin consent workflow setting.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about permission classifications in Microsoft Entra ID are true? Select TWO.
options: Only delegated permissions that don't require admin consent can be classified.
Application permissions can be classified as low impact so users can consent to them.
Classifying a permission as low grants it to all users immediately.
Classifications are stored on the service principal of the API that exposes the permission.
questions.explain: Only delegated, non-admin permissions can be classified, and the classification lives on the API's service principal (for example, Microsoft Graph). Application permissions always need admin consent. A classification only feeds consent policies and grants nothing by itself.

questions.stem: You are setting up and using the admin consent workflow. Put the steps in order.
options: Set 'Users can request admin consent to apps they are unable to consent to' to Yes
Choose the reviewers and set the request expiration in days
A user who is blocked at the consent prompt submits a request with a justification
A reviewer with a role that can grant the permissions approves the request in Admin consent requests
questions.explain: An administrator enables the workflow and configures reviewers and expiration. Only then can users submit requests from the consent prompt. Reviewers act under Admin consent requests, and they need sufficient privileges to grant the requested permissions.

questions.stem: Adatum registers a multitenant app in its own tenant. Contoso's administrator consents to it. What is created in Contoso's tenant?
options: A service principal that references Adatum's application object
A copy of the application object
A guest user account for the app
A user-assigned managed identity
questions.explain: The application object exists only in the home tenant (Adatum). Consent creates a service principal, the local instance, in Contoso's tenant. No copy of the application object, guest user or managed identity is created.

questions.stem: Which supported account type should you choose for an internal line-of-business app that only your organization's users and guests will use?
options: Multiple Entra ID tenants
Any Entra ID tenant + personal Microsoft accounts
Personal accounts only
Single tenant only
questions.explain: Single tenant (AzureADMyOrg) limits sign-in to your own tenant, including its guests, and is Microsoft's recommendation for most apps. The multitenant options let users from other organizations or with personal accounts sign in. Personal accounts only excludes your work accounts.

questions.stem: For each statement, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Registering an app in the portal also creates a service principal in the home tenant.
A managed identity's service principal has an associated application object you can edit in App registrations.
Conditional Access policies and user assignments apply to the service principal, not the application object.

questions.explain: Portal registration creates the home tenant's service principal automatically. Managed identity service principals have no editable application object. Assignments, consent grants and Conditional Access act on the service principal (the enterprise app) in each tenant.

questions.stem: A developer configures MSAL in a web app and needs the value that identifies the app in token requests. Which value from the app registration's Overview page should they use?
options: Object ID
Application (client) ID
Directory (tenant) ID
Application ID URI
questions.explain: The Application (client) ID identifies the app in authentication requests and is the same in every tenant. The Object ID is the directory object's own identifier. The tenant ID identifies the directory. The Application ID URI identifies an API the app exposes.

questions.stem: Complete the Microsoft Graph PowerShell command to create a single-tenant app registration.
options: AzureADMultipleOrgs
SingleTenant
AzureADMyOrg
PersonalMicrosoftAccount
questions.explain: signInAudience 'AzureADMyOrg' means single tenant. 'AzureADMultipleOrgs' is multitenant, and 'PersonalMicrosoftAccount' allows personal accounts only. 'SingleTenant' isn't a valid signInAudience value.

questions.stem: A GitHub Actions workflow uses workload identity federation to deploy to Azure. Put the steps of the token exchange in order.
options: The workflow requests an OIDC token from GitHub's identity provider
The workflow sends the GitHub token to the Microsoft identity platform and requests an access token
Microsoft Entra ID checks the token's issuer, subject and audience against the federated credential
Microsoft Entra ID issues an access token for the app
The workflow calls Azure Resource Manager with the access token
questions.explain: The workload first gets a token from the external IdP and presents it to Microsoft Entra ID. Entra ID validates the token against the trust (issuer, subject, audience) and issues its own access token, which the workload uses to call the Azure resource.

questions.stem: You're registering a new React single-page application that signs users in with MSAL.js. How should you configure Authentication?
options: Add the Single-page application platform with the redirect URI and leave implicit grant disabled
Add the Web platform and enable ID tokens and access tokens under implicit grant
Add the Mobile and desktop applications platform and enable public client flows
Add the Web platform and create a client secret for the browser app
questions.explain: The SPA platform uses authorization code flow with PKCE, which Microsoft recommends instead of the implicit grant. Implicit flow is discouraged. The Mobile and desktop platform is for native apps. A browser app can't keep a client secret safe.

questions.stem: Which TWO settings are configured on an app registration's Authentication blade? Select TWO.
options: Front-channel logout URL
Application ID URI
Allow public client flows
Client secret expiration
App role value
questions.explain: The Authentication blade holds platforms, redirect URIs, the front-channel logout URL, implicit grant check boxes and 'Allow public client flows'. The Application ID URI is on Expose an API, secrets are under Certificates & secrets, and app roles have their own blade.

questions.case: A command-line tool used by engineers on headless Linux servers must sign users in with the device code flow. Users get an error saying the app must be configured as a public client. The registration has a Web platform and a client secret.
questions.stem: What should you change?
options: Enable ID tokens under Implicit grant and hybrid flows
Add a front-channel logout URL
Change the supported account type to multitenant
Set Allow public client flows to Yes
questions.explain: The device code flow is a public client flow, enabled with 'Allow public client flows'. The implicit grant applies to browser token issuance, not device code. Front-channel logout handles sign-out. The account type controls which tenants can sign in, not the flow type.

questions.stem: What is the maximum lifetime you can set for a client secret on an app registration?
options: 6 months
12 months
24 months
36 months
questions.explain: Client secret lifetime is limited to 24 months, and custom lifetimes can't exceed it. Microsoft recommends setting less than 12 months and preferring certificates or federated credentials in production.

questions.stem: A GitHub Actions workflow deploys infrastructure to Azure. Security requires that no long-lived credentials are stored in GitHub. What should you configure on the app registration?
options: A client secret stored as an encrypted GitHub secret
A federated credential that trusts the repository and branch
A self-signed certificate uploaded to GitHub
A system-assigned managed identity on the GitHub runner
questions.explain: Workload identity federation lets the workflow exchange its GitHub OIDC token for an Entra token, so nothing is stored. Secrets and certificates are long-lived credentials kept in GitHub. GitHub-hosted runners aren't Azure resources, so they can't have a system-assigned managed identity.

questions.case: You add a federated credential to an app so that a Kubernetes workload can exchange its service account token for an Entra token. The issuer and subject already match the cluster's tokens.
questions.stem: Complete the credential with the recommended audience value for Microsoft Entra ID.
options: https://graph.microsoft.com
https://login.microsoftonline.com
urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer
api://AzureADTokenExchange
questions.explain: The recommended audience for federated credentials in Microsoft Entra ID is api://AzureADTokenExchange. The external token's aud claim must match it exactly. Graph and login URLs are resource and authority endpoints. The jwt-bearer URN is an OAuth assertion type, not an audience.

questions.stem: For each statement about app credentials, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Microsoft recommends certificates over client secrets for production confidential clients.
A federated credential can be added to a user-assigned managed identity.
Matching of issuer, subject and audience in a federated credential is case-insensitive.

questions.explain: Certificates are the recommended stored credential, while secrets suit testing at most. Workload identity federation can be configured on app registrations and on user-assigned managed identities. Claim matching is exact and case-sensitive, so a difference in case breaks authentication.

questions.stem: A background service runs nightly with no signed-in user and must read all users' profiles through Microsoft Graph. Which permission type does it need?
options: Application permission User.Read.All with admin consent
Delegated permission User.Read with user consent
Delegated permission User.Read.All with user consent
An exposed API scope named User.Read.All
questions.explain: With no signed-in user, the app acts as itself through the client credentials flow, which requires an application permission and admin consent. Delegated permissions need a user. Exposing a scope publishes your own API and doesn't grant Graph access.

questions.stem: You need to grant tenant-wide admin consent for the permissions configured on an app registration by using Azure CLI. Complete the command.
options: grant
add
admin-consent
approve
questions.explain: `az ad app permission admin-consent` grants admin consent for all permissions configured on the app. `add` only requests a permission on the registration. `grant` creates a delegated grant for a specific scope rather than full admin consent. `approve` isn't a valid subcommand.

questions.stem: Developers built the Orders API and need client apps to request a delegated permission named Orders.Read. Which TWO actions should you take on the Orders API registration? Select TWO.
options: Set the Application ID URI on Expose an API
Add a scope named Orders.Read on Expose an API
Create an app role named Orders.Read with Applications member type
Add Orders.Read under the API's own API permissions
Enable ID tokens under implicit grant
questions.explain: Delegated permissions are published as scopes under an Application ID URI on Expose an API. An app role with the Applications member type creates an application permission, not a delegated one. The API's own API permissions list what it consumes, not what it exposes. Implicit grant is unrelated.

questions.stem: A daemon must be granted an app role named Orders.Process as an application permission. Complete the manifest entry for the role.
options: "User"
"Application"
"ServicePrincipal"
"Daemon"
questions.explain: allowedMemberTypes "Application" makes the role show up as an application permission that client apps can request. "User" covers users and groups only. "ServicePrincipal" and "Daemon" aren't valid values.

questions.stem: In which token claim does Microsoft Entra ID put the app roles assigned to a user?
options: scp
groups
wids
roles
questions.explain: Assigned app roles appear in the roles claim using each role's Value. scp holds delegated scopes, groups holds group object IDs, and wids lists Entra directory role template IDs.

questions.case: The Survey app registration defines an app role with display name 'Survey Writer', value 'Survey.Create' and allowed member types 'Users/Groups'. A developer also wants a reporting daemon to receive this role.
questions.stem: For each statement, select Yes if true.

statements.s: The daemon can be granted the role under API permissions > My APIs > Application permissions as currently configured.
The app's code should check the roles claim for the string 'Survey.Create', not 'Survey Writer'.
Disabling the role prevents new assignments, but existing assignments still appear in tokens until you remove them.

questions.explain: With Users/Groups only, the role doesn't appear as an application permission. Change it to Applications or Both. The roles claim carries the Value, not the display name. A disabled role can't be assigned again, but existing assignments still appear in tokens until you remove them.

questions.stem: You want ongoing cloud discovery of apps used on corporate laptops, both on and off the corporate network, without deploying a log collector. What should you use?
options: The Microsoft Defender for Endpoint integration
Snapshot reports uploaded weekly
A Docker-based log collector on the corporate network
The Microsoft 365 app connector
questions.explain: The Defender for Endpoint integration feeds continuous discovery from the devices themselves, wherever they are. Snapshot reports are manual, one-off uploads. A log collector sees only traffic through corporate appliances. App connectors show activity inside connected apps, not discovery.

questions.stem: With the Defender for Endpoint integration and Enforce app access enabled, you want users who visit a file-sharing app to see a warning they can bypass, without being fully blocked. Which tag should you apply to the app?
options: Sanctioned
Unsanctioned
Monitored
Custom tag named Warn
questions.explain: Apps tagged Monitored produce a warning with a bypass option on Defender for Endpoint devices. Unsanctioned apps are blocked. Sanctioned apps are approved and not restricted. A custom tag has no enforcement behavior.

questions.stem: Which TWO are valid ways to feed continuous cloud discovery reports in Defender for Cloud Apps? Select TWO.
options: A log collector receiving firewall logs over Syslog or FTP
Manually uploading a proxy log as a snapshot report
Microsoft Entra sign-in logs exported to a storage account
Integration with a supported secure web gateway such as Zscaler
The Microsoft Purview audit log
questions.explain: Continuous reports come from a log collector, Defender for Endpoint, or secure web gateway integrations such as Zscaler, iboss, Corrata and Menlo Security. Manual uploads create snapshot reports. Entra sign-in logs and the Purview audit log aren't cloud discovery traffic sources.

questions.stem: You must block an unsanctioned cloud storage app on managed Windows devices by using Defender for Cloud Apps and Defender for Endpoint. Put the steps in order.
options: Enable Enforce app access and custom network indicators for the integration
Tag the discovered app as Unsanctioned
Defender for Cloud Apps syncs the app's domains to Defender for Endpoint as custom URL indicators
Network protection in block mode blocks the domain on devices
questions.explain: The integration settings must be on before tags have any effect. Tagging the app Unsanctioned triggers the sync of its domains as custom URL indicators, and Defender Antivirus network protection in block mode then enforces them on devices.

questions.stem: Your company sanctioned Box. You need to scan files already stored in Box for sensitive data and quarantine matches automatically. What should you configure first?
options: A Conditional Access app control session policy for Box
Box tagged as Monitored in the cloud app catalog
A Box app connector in Defender for Cloud Apps
App-enforced restrictions in a Conditional Access policy
questions.explain: Scanning data at rest and governance actions such as quarantine need API access through an app connector. Session policies act only on live browser sessions. Tags affect discovery enforcement. App-enforced restrictions work only for supported Microsoft 365 apps.

questions.stem: For each statement about app connectors, select Yes if true.

statements.s: App connectors use the connected app provider's APIs.
App connectors control downloads in real time during a browser session.
Connecting Microsoft 365 provides visibility into OAuth apps that users have authorized.

questions.explain: Connectors are API-based and work out of band, so real-time session control comes from Conditional Access app control. The Microsoft 365 connector supplies app permission data, which drives the OAuth apps page and OAuth app policies.

questions.stem: Which Defender for Cloud Apps capability lets you automatically suspend a Salesforce user account when a policy detects mass report exports?
options: A cloud discovery anomaly detection policy
A Salesforce app connector with a governance action
An access policy with the Block action
An app discovery policy that tags Salesforce Unsanctioned
questions.explain: Account governance actions, such as suspending a user, depend on an app connector that has API access to the app. Cloud discovery policies work only on traffic logs. Access policies block sign-in sessions but don't suspend accounts. Tagging Salesforce Unsanctioned would block the whole app.

questions.stem: Users on unmanaged devices must be able to view SharePoint Online documents in the browser but not download, print or sync them. You want the simplest solution with no reverse proxy. What should you use?
options: A Conditional Access policy that requires a compliant device
A Defender for Cloud Apps access policy with the Block action
A Conditional Access policy with the sign-in frequency session control
SharePoint limited web-only access for unmanaged devices with the 'Use app enforced restrictions' session control
questions.explain: App-enforced restrictions let SharePoint itself give unmanaged devices a web-only, no-download experience. Requiring a compliant device blocks access entirely. An access policy blocks the whole session. Sign-in frequency only controls how often users reauthenticate.

questions.stem: Complete the SharePoint Online PowerShell command so that unmanaged devices get browser-only access with no downloads.
options: BlockAccess
AllowFullAccess
AllowLimitedAccess
ReadOnly
questions.explain: AllowLimitedAccess gives limited, web-only access from unmanaged devices and works with app-enforced restrictions. AllowFullAccess removes the restriction and BlockAccess blocks unmanaged devices completely. ReadOnly is a value for Set-OwaMailboxPolicy in Exchange Online, not for SharePoint.

questions.case: Fabrikam uses app-enforced restrictions to limit SharePoint Online on unmanaged devices. Management now wants the same 'view but don't download' behavior for Salesforce and for a third-party HR SaaS app, both federated with Microsoft Entra ID through SAML.
questions.stem: What should you implement for those two apps?
options: Conditional Access app control with a session policy that blocks downloads on unmanaged devices
Add both apps to the existing Conditional Access policy that uses app enforced restrictions
Tag both apps as Monitored in cloud discovery
Set 'Visible to users?' to No on both enterprise apps
questions.explain: App-enforced restrictions work only in apps that support them, mainly SharePoint, OneDrive and Exchange Online. For other SAML apps, Conditional Access app control with a download-control session policy is needed. Monitored tags affect endpoint discovery warnings, and visibility only hides tiles.

questions.stem: Where do you enable routing of a user's session to Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps for real-time session control?
options: In a Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policy, under Session > Use Conditional Access App Control
On the enterprise app's Properties page, by setting Assignment required to Yes
In the Defender for Cloud Apps cloud app catalog, by tagging the app Sanctioned
In Microsoft Intune, with an app protection policy
questions.explain: Conditional Access app control starts with the Entra Conditional Access session control 'Use Conditional Access App Control'. Assignment settings, catalog tags and Intune app protection policies don't route sessions to Defender for Cloud Apps.

questions.stem: For each statement about Conditional Access app control, select Yes if true.

statements.s: In browsers other than Microsoft Edge, protected app URLs get a .mcas.ms suffix.
It requires an agent to be installed on each user's device.
Apps that use Microsoft Entra ID for SAML or OIDC single sign-on are onboarded automatically.

questions.explain: Other browsers are reverse-proxied with the .mcas.ms suffix, while Edge for Business uses in-browser protection. No device agent is needed, which suits BYOD devices. Entra ID apps onboard automatically, and apps on non-Microsoft IdPs need manual onboarding.

questions.case: Contoso applies session policies to Salesforce through Conditional Access app control. Auditors find that users bypass the download controls by signing in with the Salesforce mobile app, which session controls don't cover.
questions.stem: What should you do?
options: Create a session policy with Control file upload set to Block
Create a Defender for Cloud Apps access policy that blocks the Mobile and desktop client app type for Salesforce
Tag Salesforce as Unsanctioned in cloud discovery
Enable app-enforced restrictions for Salesforce
questions.explain: Session controls apply to browser sessions, so the fix is an access policy that blocks native mobile and desktop clients and forces browser access. An upload control doesn't address downloads. Unsanctioning blocks the whole app. Salesforce doesn't support app-enforced restrictions.

questions.stem: Users on unmanaged devices may keep working in SharePoint through the browser. When they download a file labeled Confidential, it must be encrypted automatically. Which session policy configuration meets this?
options: Session control type Monitor only
Session control type Block activities with an activity filter for Print
An access policy with the Audit action
Session control type Control file download (with inspection) with the Protect action
questions.explain: The Protect action on a download-control session policy applies a sensitivity label with encryption as the file downloads. Monitor only logs sign-ins. Block activities stops activities instead of protecting files. An access policy decides only whether a session is allowed.

questions.stem: Which TWO session control types can you choose when creating a Defender for Cloud Apps session policy? Select TWO.
options: Block activities
Require password change
Control file upload (with inspection)
Require compliant device
Revoke OAuth app
questions.explain: Session control types are Monitor only, Block activities, Control file download (with inspection) and Control file upload (with inspection). Require password change and Require compliant device are Entra Conditional Access grant controls. Revoking OAuth apps is an OAuth app policy action.

questions.case: Woodgrove Bank requires that users on devices that aren't Intune compliant can't use Workday at all. Users on compliant devices can use Workday, but downloads of files containing credit card numbers must be blocked. Workday is federated with Microsoft Entra ID and routed through Conditional Access app control.
questions.stem: Which TWO Defender for Cloud Apps policies should you create? Select TWO.
options: An access policy that blocks sessions from devices without the Intune compliant tag
A session policy that controls file download with content inspection and the Block action
An OAuth app policy that revokes Workday
An app discovery policy that tags Workday as Unsanctioned
A session policy with Monitor only
questions.explain: The access policy blocks noncompliant devices at sign-in. A download-control session policy with inspection blocks files containing card numbers for allowed users. OAuth and discovery policies would disrupt all Workday use. Monitor only doesn't block anything.

questions.stem: You want an alert, and automatic revocation, when a rarely used third-party app that requests high permissions is authorized by users in your Microsoft 365 tenant. What should you create in Defender for Cloud Apps?
options: An OAuth app policy filtered on permission level High and community use Rare
An app discovery policy filtered on risk score
A session policy with Block activities
A file policy on SharePoint Online
questions.explain: OAuth app policies evaluate authorized apps by permission level, community use and the number of authorizing users, and they can revoke apps. Discovery policies look at traffic logs. Session policies act on live sessions. File policies scan content.

questions.stem: For each statement about OAuth apps in Defender for Cloud Apps, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Marking an OAuth app as Approved changes what end users can do with it.
OAuth app governance covers apps authorized in Microsoft 365, Google Workspace and Salesforce.
App governance is included with a Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps license.

questions.explain: Approve is only a review marker with no effect on users, while Ban disables the app. OAuth app visibility covers Microsoft 365, Google Workspace and Salesforce. App governance comes with a Defender for Cloud Apps license and is turned on in Cloud Apps settings.

questions.case: An investigation finds that 120 users consented to a malicious OAuth app that reads their mailboxes. You must stop the app's current access, and you must stop users from consenting to unverified apps in the future.
questions.stem: Which TWO actions should you take? Select TWO.
options: Ban the app on the OAuth apps page in Defender for Cloud Apps
Tag the app as Unsanctioned in the cloud app catalog
Set Entra user consent to allow only verified publishers with low-impact permissions
Create a session policy that blocks Outlook downloads
Add the app to a My Apps collection
questions.explain: Banning the OAuth app disables the enterprise app and cuts its API access. Restricting user consent in Entra prevents future consent to unverified apps. Unsanctioning is a discovery control for traffic and doesn't affect OAuth API access. Session policies don't touch app-only API calls, and collections are cosmetic.

questions.stem: In the Defender for Cloud Apps cloud app catalog, which four categories make up an app's risk score?
options: Identity, Device, Network, Data
General, Security, Compliance, Legal
Availability, Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy
Popularity, Usage, Traffic, Location
questions.explain: The catalog scores apps on more than 90 risk factors grouped into General, Security, Compliance and Legal, and the total is a weighted average of those categories. The other groupings sound plausible but aren't the catalog's categories.

questions.stem: Your compliance team cares more about legal data-ownership terms than about company age when evaluating apps. How can you make discovered apps' risk scores reflect this?
options: Request a score update for every app in the catalog
Create a custom app tag named Legal-Priority
Adjust the category and field weights in Cloud Discovery Score metrics
Generate a new snapshot report
questions.explain: Score metrics let you change the weight of risk categories and fields, or ignore some, so scores match your priorities. A score update request fixes wrong app data. Custom tags only label apps. A new snapshot report reuses the same scoring.

questions.stem: Which Microsoft Entra capability lets users request a bundle of group membership, app access and SharePoint Online site access that is approved and then expires automatically?
options: An access package in entitlement management
A dynamic membership group
An administrative unit
A lifecycle workflow
questions.explain: Access packages bundle resource roles with request, approval and expiry policies. Dynamic groups assign by attribute with no request or approval. Administrative units scope admin permissions. Lifecycle workflows automate joiner/mover/leaver tasks, not self-service requests.

questions.stem: Your tenant has Microsoft Entra ID P2 licences. You want an access package to be assigned automatically to every user whose department is Sales and removed when they leave Sales. What licence do you need?
options: No extra licence; Microsoft Entra ID P2 covers it
Microsoft Entra ID Governance
Microsoft Entra Workload ID Premium
Microsoft Intune Plan 1
questions.explain: Automatic assignment policies are an ID Governance feature; P2 covers core entitlement management such as requests and approvals but not auto-assignment. Workload ID Premium is for workload identities, and Intune licences are for device management.

questions.stem: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

statements.s: An access package can contain resources from more than one catalog.
A single access package can have several policies, for example one for employees and one for partners.
When a user's access package assignment ends, the resource roles granted by that package are removed.

questions.explain: Each access package belongs to exactly one catalog and uses resources from it. Packages can have multiple policies for different populations. Ending an assignment removes the access the package granted.

questions.stem: A team lead must add and remove users from existing access packages in the Marketing catalog and manage their requests. The lead must not create or edit access packages. Which role should you assign?
options: Access package manager
Catalog owner
Access package assignment manager
Catalog reader
